Locally, Makamba's low tourism, distance from the capital and international organisations, conservative community structures and limited oversight mean fewer protective institutions or recourse if a visitor is outed, and no known local exception to national law and practice.

regions.name: Muramvya
regions.basis: Muramvya is a central province of Burundi, where the national penal code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with imprisonment of three months to two years and a fine, and where no legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection, or recognised LGBTIQ association registration is available. Enforcement has included arrests, investigations, and, in 2023, convictions with prison sentences, while official rhetoric in December 2023 from the president likened gay sex to satanic choice and suggested stoning, prompting reports of fear and perceived licence for killing among LGBTQ Burundians. No region-specific information distinguishes Muramvya from the national picture: there is no documented local exception, protective practice, or tolerance regime, and a transgender visitor discovered there would face the same criminal exposure, societal hostility, and lack of recourse.

regions.name: Muyinga
regions.basis: Muyinga is a rural northern province of Burundi, where a transgender visitor conditional on discovery would face the national legal regime: same-sex conduct is criminalised with imprisonment and fines, there is no legal gender recognition or protection from discrimination based on gender identity, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register. Enforcement intensified in 2023 with arrests and prison sentences, and senior officials have publicly endorsed violent punishment, creating a climate of societal hostility and impunity. No region-specific information distinguishes Muyinga from the national picture regarding border practice, facilities, custody, health care, or recourse for trans visitors.

regions.name: Mwaro
regions.basis: A transgender visitor in Mwaro would be subject to Burundi's national regime, under which consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised with penalties of three months to two years' imprisonment and a fine, there is no legal gender recognition or government protection against discrimination based on gender identity, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register. Enforcement intensified in 2023 with arrests and prison sentences, and in December 2023 the president publicly endorsed stoning people for gay sex, reported to have produced terror and perceived license for violence among LGBTQ Burundians. Harassment, family rejection and societal discrimination are documented nationally. No region-specific information distinguishes Mwaro from the national picture in enforcement, protection, or tolerance.

regions.name: Ngozi
regions.basis: Burundi criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under its Penal Code, punishable by imprisonment and fines, with documented arrests, convictions and police extortion since 2009 and intensified enforcement in 2023. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register. In December 2023 the president publicly endorsed stoning people engaging in gay sex, which Burundian activists described as a license to kill amid wider extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and torture. No region-specific information distinguishes Ngozi from the national picture; no local protective exception or different enforcement regime is known.

regions.name: Rumonge
regions.basis: Rumonge is a coastal province of Burundi where national law criminalises same-sex conduct with imprisonment and fines, provides no legal gender recognition, no protection from discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and does not permit LGBTIQ organisations to register. Enforcement has included arrests, extortion, prosecutions and prison sentences, intensifying in 2023, and senior officials have publicly expressed hostility, including calls for violence. No region-specific information distinguishes Rumonge from the national picture regarding border screening, facilities, policing, health care or social treatment of transgender visitors, and no local protective measures are known.

regions.name: Rutana
regions.basis: Rutana is a small rural province in southern Burundi, where same-sex sexual conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code, punishable by up to two years in prison and a fine, and there is no legal gender recognition or government protection against discrimination based on gender identity. Documented enforcement includes arrests, prosecutions and convictions, and in December 2023 the president publicly endorsed stoning people engaging in gay sex, remarks that LGBTQ Burundians described as a licence for lethal violence. No region-specific information distinguishes Rutana from the national picture; the same criminalisation, official hostility and lack of recourse would apply to a transgender visitor discovered there.

regions.name: Ruyigi
regions.basis: Ruyigi is a largely rural province in eastern Burundi. No region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture, and no distinct local enforcement practice, protective measure, or trans-specific incident is known for the province. The applicable national regime criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with imprisonment of three months to two years and fines, provides no legal gender recognition, and bars registration of LGBTIQ organisations. Enforcement has included arrests, extortion for release, and, in 2023, convictions with one to two year sentences. In December 2023 the president publicly endorsed stoning people engaging in gay sex, after which LGBTQ Burundians reported terror. LGBT people face societal discrimination with no government protection, in a context of arbitrary arrests and extrajudicial violence.

regions.name: Atlanique
regions.basis: Atlanique, centred on Cotonou, is Benin's southern coastal and most urbanised department and its economic capital, with greater anonymity, business and foreign presence than rural areas where hostility is reported as strongest. Nationally, consensual adult same-sex conduct is legal, but there is no protection based on gender identity, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Routine refusal of hormone and general medical care, religious framing of transgender people, and civilian anti-gay lynchings described as commonplace with police rarely pursuing perpetrators apply across the country. Cotonou has hosted public gatherings and small survivor-support accommodation, yet no department-level protection distinguishes visitors from the national pattern of impunity and service denial.

regions.name: Borgou
regions.basis: Borgou, centered on Parakou in north-eastern Benin, inherits Benin's national regime, where same-sex conduct between adults is legal but there is no legal recognition or anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, medical and other service denials are documented, and civilian violence is rarely punished. Locally, Borgou is more rural and predominantly Muslim than the southern coast, with a more socially and religiously conservative population outside Parakou, weaker access to the few support and shelter services concentrated in the south, and less tourism-oriented infrastructure. A visitor who is outed there faces greater likelihood of hostile social reaction, refusal of care, and little effective recourse from local police or services, with distance from Cotonou compounding isolation.

regions.name: Littoral
regions.basis: Littoral, centered on Cotonou and Porto-Novo, is Benin's most urban coastal department, with the main port, airport, universities, foreign residents, and denser, more anonymous street life than rural Benin. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is not criminalized, but there is no legal protection based on gender identity, no legal gender recognition, and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity. If outed, a visitor can face refusal of medical and other services, including hormone treatment, harassment, and civilian violence that is rarely prosecuted. Religious preaching frames transgender people negatively, while small LGBT support accommodation exists in the urban area. Cotonou's cosmopolitan character may reduce overt rural hostility, but it does not provide enforceable recourse.

regions.name: Oueme
regions.basis: Oueme, a southern coastal department in Benin, is assessed under Benin's national regime, and no region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture. Consensual adult same-sex acts are legal, but indecency provisions have been used to prosecute same-sex conduct, and there is no legal protection on grounds of gender identity, no anti-discrimination law, and no legal gender recognition. Trans visitors face documented refusal of medical and social services, including general care, and employer exclusion. Hostility is documented especially outside major urban areas, with anti-gay lynchings described as commonplace and police rarely pursuing perpetrators, while victims fear mistreatment if they report. Religious actors are documented as a significant source of hostility and coerced conversion practices. Small survivor-support shelters exist, but LGBTI organisations cannot register.

regions.name: Centre
regions.basis: Centre, centred on Ouagadougou, is Burkina Faso's capital and largest city, concentrating the government, police headquarters, main international airport, embassies and major hospitals, with denser checkpoints and document scrutiny than rural areas. No regional law, protective practice or documented local exception distinguishes it from the national regime. Since September 2025 that regime criminalises same-sex acts with imprisonment and fines, bans promotion, and provides for deportation of foreign nationals, with no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity and no documented response to anti-LGBT violence. Urban anonymity and a larger foreign presence may reduce everyday notice, but proximity to state institutions increases the likelihood that discovery leads to detention or removal.

regions.name: Centre-Est
regions.basis: Burkina Faso criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with two to five years' imprisonment and fines under the criminal code effective 1 September 2025, with foreign nationals subject to deportation, and prohibits promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour. A trans visitor whose relationship or presentation is read locally as same-sex conduct therefore faces statutory exposure on discovery, in a society where religious and traditional opinion is hostile and no mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented, amid reported fear of a witch hunt and self-censorship. No region-specific information distinguishes Centre-Est from the national picture.

regions.name: Centre-Nord
regions.basis: A transgender visitor in Centre-Nord, centred on Kaya, falls under Burkina Faso's national regime, in force since September 2025, which criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with two to five years' imprisonment and fines, bans promotion, and provides for deportation of foreign nationals. The constitution and anti-discrimination provisions make no reference to sexual orientation or gender identity, and no mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented. Societal discrimination and religious and traditional non-acceptance are reported, alongside fear of a witch hunt and self-censorship following criminalisation, with no arrests reported in the initial weeks. No region-specific information distinguishes Centre-Nord from the national picture.

regions.name: Centre-Ouest
regions.basis: Centre-Ouest inherits Burkina Faso's national framework, with no region-specific information distinguishing how transgender visitors are treated there from the national picture. Consensual same-sex conduct became criminal in September 2025, carrying two to five years' imprisonment and a fine, with deportation stated for foreign nationals, and promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour is also prohibited. A transgender visitor whose relationship is read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status could fall within those terms if discovered. No arrests had been reported by late September 2025, but reporting described fear and self-censorship. The constitution's anti-discrimination clause omits sexual orientation and gender identity, and no mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented.

regions.name: Centre-Sud
regions.basis: Burkina Faso criminalised consensual same-sex conduct from 1 September 2025, with two to five years' imprisonment and fines, promotion offences, and deportation stated for foreign nationals; a trans visitor in a relationship read under birth sex as same-sex falls within those terms if discovered. The constitution's anti-discrimination clause omits sexual orientation and gender identity, and no mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented. Centre-Sud is a largely rural region centred on Manga, with no documented local exception, protective regime, or distinct enforcement practice distinguishing it from the national picture; no region-specific information distinguishes it from the national regime.

regions.name: Hauts-Bassins
regions.basis: Hauts-Bassins inherits Burkina Faso's national regime, under which consensual same-sex relations became a criminal offence on 1 September 2025, punishable by two to five years' imprisonment and a fine, with foreign nationals subject to deportation, and promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour also prohibited. A transgender visitor whose relationship is read locally on the basis of sex assigned at birth would fall within those terms. The constitution's anti-discrimination clause omits sexual orientation and gender identity, and no mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented, while religious and traditional opinion has not accepted homosexuality and societal abuse has been reported. No region-specific information distinguishes Hauts-Bassins, including Bobo-Dioulasso, from the national picture on enforcement or protection.

regions.name: Barisal
regions.basis: Barisal Division in south-central Bangladesh is a largely rural, riverine, overwhelmingly Muslim region with limited foreign tourism and few large-city support or legal-aid networks compared with Dhaka. No Barisal-specific law, protective programme, or tourism exception distinguishes it from the national regime. Bangladesh retains Penal Code Section 377 criminalising consensual same-sex intercourse with imprisonment up to life, police documented using it and suspicious-behaviour provisions to harass effeminate and visibly gender-nonconforming people, with extortion, arbitrary arrest, and retaliatory violence in 2025. Third-gender recognition since 2013 applies mainly to hijra identity without general protection against discrimination or violence. If outed, a visitor would face social hostility, police harassment or extortion, possible detention, and very limited effective recourse locally.

regions.name: Mymensingh
regions.basis: A transgender visitor in Mymensingh encounters Bangladesh's national regime, under which same-sex conduct remains punishable under Penal Code Section 377, with documented police use of the provision and related public-order powers for harassment, extortion, raids and arrests of visibly gender-nonconforming people, including at transit points. Hijra identity has been recognised as third gender since 2013 and appears on voter lists, but there is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and recognition has not produced broader legal safeguards. Reported violence, assault, extortion and arbitrary arrest against LGBTQI+ people increased nationally in recent years amid Islamist mobilisation. No region-specific information distinguishes Mymensingh from the national picture.

regions.name: Kardzhali
regions.basis: Kardzhali inherits Bulgaria's national regime: gender identity and expression are not criminalised, no law governs facility use by gender, and a foreign passport draws no separate border question, while legal gender recognition is closed domestically and anti-discrimination protections remain incomplete with documented failures to investigate bias crimes, alongside 2024 education restrictions on promotion of non-traditional orientation and gender identity. Locally, this southern province is largely rural and predominantly ethnic Turkish and Muslim, with socially conservative, close-knit communities, limited international tourism and little visible LGBT infrastructure compared with Sofia or Plovdiv. A visitor who is outed would therefore face greater social friction and fewer informal supports or remedies, though no region-specific criminal or border regime distinguishes it.

regions.name: Ruse
regions.basis: Ruse is a Danube university and border city in northeastern Bulgaria, where a transgender visitor encountered after discovery faces the national regime: no criminal offence for gender identity or expression and no statute governing facility use, and foreign passports examined on ordinary terms with no separate gender-identity entry rule. Protection against discrimination covers sex including sex change in housing, education and health care, but not explicitly gender identity, and hate-crime investigation has repeatedly failed in practice. A 2024 education law bans promotion of non-traditional orientation or gender identity beyond biology, and legal gender recognition remains closed for residents. No region-specific information distinguishes Ruse from the national picture on policing, facilities, care or public reaction, and social tolerance remains contested with public visibility dependent on police protection.

regions.name: Smolyan
regions.basis: Smolyan is a small mountain town and provincial capital in Bulgaria's southern Rhodope region, with a largely rural, domestically oriented visitor economy and no known specialist LGBTQ venues or support organisations. A foreign passport is treated on ordinary terms, gender identity and expression are not criminalised, and no law governs facility use by gender. Legal gender recognition is closed for residents, anti-discrimination protection is incomplete, and hate-crime enforcement is weak. Local attitudes are generally more socially conservative than in Sofia, with less anonymity and recourse farther from national legal and advocacy support, while there is no documented distinct local travel regime.

regions.name: Capital Governorate
regions.basis: Capital Governorate, centred on Manama and its Juffair and Seef hotel and business districts, holds Bahrain's government, courts, main police headquarters and much of its expatriate and visitor population. The national morality and indecency provisions, entry screening for suspected effeminate or LGBTQ visitors, and deportation for non-Bahrainis apply in full here, with courts in Manama rejecting legal gender recognition except after surgery or medical necessity. Visitor anonymity in international hotels and expatriate areas offers some discretion, but centralised police presence, hotel registration and document checks increase exposure, and there are no anti-discrimination protections or LGBTQ organisations to provide recourse if a visitor is outed.

regions.name: Biminis
regions.basis: The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 1991 and imposes no imprisonment for being transgender, but gender identity has no protection in anti-discrimination or hate-crime law, marriage is defined by sex at birth, and senior politicians have publicly called for transgender people to leave. Social attitudes are strongly conservative, with documented anti-gay violence, gay-panic acquittances and unsolved killings and little recourse. Bimini is a small, close-knit island community dependent on tourism, ferries and a single small clinic and police presence. There are no locally known protective measures, anonymity is limited, and help if outed would be constrained by the island's size and remoteness.

regions.name: Black Point
regions.basis: Black Point is a small settlement on Great Guana Cay in the Abacos, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture in the Bahamas. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity is not covered by anti-discrimination or hate-crime law, so employment, housing, healthcare and public services can be denied without legal remedy. Official statements have included calls to exile transgender people, and social attitudes are strongly conservative, with LGBT visibility largely private and underground. A gay visitor was beaten at a major tourist event in 2017 without bias-crime charges available. In a small community, being recognised would likely draw intense local attention with limited recourse.

regions.name: Central Andros
regions.basis: Central Andros is a small, remote Family Island district in the Bahamas with limited tourism, medical and police infrastructure and a tightly knit, socially conservative community. It shares the national legal position: consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity is not covered by anti-discrimination or hate-crime laws, marriage is defined by sex at birth, and political leaders have expressed hostility toward transgender people. With no local protections, limited recourse after harassment or violence, and little anonymity in a small community, a visitor who is recognised as transgender faces social hostility, service denial and possible violence with little practical remedy, while everyday official interaction is less frequent than in Nassau.

regions.name: Central Eleuthera
regions.basis: Central Eleuthera is a rural island district in the Bahamas, where transgender visitors fall under the national legal framework. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity has no protection in anti-discrimination, harassment or hate-crime law, marriage is defined by sex at birth, and political figures have publicly called for transgender people to be exiled. Social attitudes are shaped by conservative Christian communities, LGBT visibility is constrained, and past anti-gay violence has not been treated as bias crime. No region-specific information distinguishes Central Eleuthera from the national picture, and no local protective or hostile exception is known.

regions.name: City of Freeport
regions.basis: City of Freeport, on Grand Bahama, operates under the Bahamas' national laws, which decriminalised consensual adult same-sex conduct in 1991 but provide no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on gender identity, with marriage defined by sex at birth and no recognised route for visitors to remedy discrimination in housing, employment, healthcare or public services. Political and social opposition to transgender inclusion is documented nationally, alongside conservative Christian attitudes, underground social life, and past anti-gay violence and gay-panic acquittals without bias-crime charging. Freeport's cruise and resort tourism brings high visitor volume, but no region-specific information distinguishes its legal protections, policing or social treatment from the national picture.

regions.name: Grand Cay
regions.basis: Grand Cay is a small, remote, tight-knit fishing community in the Abaco islands, reached by ferry and with limited lodging, healthcare, policing depth and legal assistance compared with Nassau. The Bahamas has decriminalised consensual adult same-sex conduct and has no trans-specific criminal offence, but provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on gender identity, and senior political figures have publicly called for transgender people to be exiled. Social attitudes are strongly conservative, LGBT life is largely hidden, and bias-motivated violence has been treated leniently. On a small island, discovery would be difficult to escape, alternative services and recourse are scarce, and dependence on limited transport increases exposure.

regions.name: Hope Town
regions.basis: Hope Town is a small, affluent tourism settlement on Elbow Cay in the Abaco Islands, dependent on foreign visitors and second-home owners, with a quiet, orderly, low-crime character and limited nightlife. Bahamian national law applies throughout: consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on gender identity, marriage is defined by sex at birth, and political figures have expressed hostility toward transgender people. Wider Bahamian society is socially conservative and largely disapproving, and documented homophobic violence has occurred elsewhere in the country without bias-crime recourse. In Hope Town itself, visitor-oriented tolerance and low local enforcement likely reduce everyday confrontation, yet a transgender visitor who is outed would have no specific legal protection.

regions.name: Mangrove Cay
regions.basis: Mangrove Cay is a small, remote settlement on Andros, far from Nassau's tourist infrastructure, hospitals, lawyers and advocacy organisations. A transgender visitor outed there would face the Bahamas' national position: adult consensual same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, marriage is defined by sex at birth, and senior political figures have promoted exclusion of transgender people. In a tight-knit, conservative Christian community with little anonymity and few places to change lodging, make a complaint or obtain care, discovery would be highly visible and difficult to escape locally. Documented gay-panic acquittals and overwhelming social disapproval nationally, with an underground rather than public scene, leave little practical recourse if harassment or violence occurs.

regions.name: Moore's Island
regions.basis: A transgender visitor to Moore's Island encounters the Bahamas' national legal framework, which decriminalised consensual adult same-sex conduct in 1991 but provides no protection against discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, healthcare, banking or public businesses, and no hate-crime law covering anti-trans or anti-gay violence. Official statements have included calls to exile transgender people, social attitudes are strongly conservative, and advocacy groups note the absence of legal protection. No region-specific information distinguishes Moore's Island from the national picture on border treatment, facilities, policing, detention or healthcare for transgender visitors.

regions.name: New Providence
regions.basis: New Providence, containing Nassau and Paradise Island, is the capital and principal tourist centre, with large resorts, cruise terminals and hotels, giving a transgender visitor more anonymity and tourist-oriented services than smaller islands, but national law applies without local exception. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, yet gender identity has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, the same-sex age of consent is higher, and marriage is defined by sex at birth. Political figures have publicly called for transgender people to be exiled, social attitudes are strongly conservative Christian, and the Nassau scene is largely hidden. A gay visitor was beaten at Junkanoo Carnival in Nassau in 2017, police raided a gay party there in 2007, and gay-panic defences have succeeded in court, leaving harassment, service discrimination and violence with little recourse.

regions.name: North Abaco
regions.basis: North Abaco is governed by the same national framework that applies throughout the Bahamas, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity is not covered by anti-discrimination or hate-crime law, so discrimination and bias-motivated violence have no specific statutory remedy. Political statements have included calls to exclude transgender people, courts have shown leniency toward gay-panic claims, and social attitudes remain strongly conservative, with LGBT life largely kept private. If a visitor is outed, exposure is therefore to harassment, discrimination, and possible violence without dedicated legal protection, rather than to criminal penalties for identity itself.

regions.name: North Andros
regions.basis: The Bahamas decriminalised consensual adult same-sex conduct in 1991 but provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing, healthcare, banking or public businesses, has no hate-crime law, and retains an 18-year age of consent for same-sex acts compared with 16 for opposite-sex acts. Political hostility has included calls to exile transgender people, while social attitudes remain strongly conservative and LGBT visibility is largely hidden. North Andros is a rural, settlement-based island with limited tourism infrastructure compared with Nassau, small communities where a visitor is more readily noticed, and limited hospital, police and legal resources. Discovery there would therefore be more locally visible and harder to remedy, with no known local protections distinguishing it from the national pattern.

regions.name: North Eleuthera
regions.basis: North Eleuthera is a small, sparsely populated Bahamian island district whose visitors encounter the national regime: consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity has no protection in anti-discrimination, harassment or hate-crime law, marriage is defined by sex at birth, and official rhetoric has included calls to exile transgender people. Social attitudes are shaped by conservative Christian denominations and strong public disapproval, with LGBT life largely private and underground, and past anti-gay violence has not been treated as bias crime. No region-specific information distinguishes North Eleuthera from the national picture on border treatment, facilities, healthcare or policing, so no local difference in enforcement or recourse is documented.

regions.name: Rum Cay
regions.basis: Rum Cay is a small, remote Bahamian island with a tiny settled community and limited visitor infrastructure, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture. The Bahamas decriminalised consensual adult same-sex conduct but provides no protection against gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing, healthcare or public services, and no hate-crime law. Political leaders have expressed hostility toward transgender people, social attitudes are strongly conservative, and an underground scene in Nassau offers no local equivalent. The 2017 beating of a gay visitor at a major event, unsolved murders, and lenient judicial responses illustrate limited recourse if a visitor is discovered.

regions.name: San Salvador
regions.basis: San Salvador is assessed under the Bahamas national regime, and no region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity is absent from anti-discrimination and hate-crime law, the Constitution does not cover it, and marriage is defined by sex at birth. Documented political calls to exclude transgender people, widespread conservative Christian social disapproval, underground social life, and a documented beating of a gay visitor at a major tourist event without bias-crime recourse indicate that a visitor who is outed may face harassment, service exclusion, or violence with limited legal remedy, while imprisonment for being transgender is not documented.

regions.name: South Abaco
regions.basis: South Abaco offers no separate legal regime from the rest of the Bahamas. Adult consensual same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but gender identity has no protection in anti-discrimination, harassment or hate-crime law, and marriage law is defined by sex at birth. Political figures have publicly called for transgender people to be exiled, advocacy groups report an absence of legal protection, and conservative Christian attitudes and high disapproval of same-sex relationships shape social reception. A gay visitor was beaten during a tourist carnival and charged without a bias-crime framework. No region-specific information distinguishes South Abaco from the national picture.

regions.name: South Andros
regions.basis: South Andros is a sparsely populated Family Island community in the Bahamas, with small settlements, limited health and police services, and a close-knit, socially conservative population where a visitor is readily noticed. It inherits the national position: consensual adult same-sex conduct is decriminalised, but there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection for gender identity, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman at birth, and senior political figures have expressed hostile views toward transgender people. Social disapproval is strong, LGBT visibility is constrained, and recourse for bias-motivated harassment or violence is limited and centred far away in Nassau. No local protective regime distinguishes the island.

regions.name: South Eleuthera
regions.basis: South Eleuthera is a remote, low-population Family Island district of small settlements such as Rock Sound and Governor's Harbour, with limited tourism infrastructure compared with Nassau and a close-knit, socially conservative Christian community where visitors are readily noticeable. It operates under the Bahamas' national regime: consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1991, but gender identity receives no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection in employment, housing, health care or public services, and senior political figures have publicly called for transgender people to be exiled. Documented gay-panic acquittals, a 2017 beating of a gay visitor at a carnival, underground nightlife and widespread disapproval shape the context, with legal, medical and advocacy support concentrated in Nassau and distant from southern Eleuthera.

regions.name: Brčko District
regions.basis: Brčko District is a self-governing, neutral, multi-ethnic district in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina, outside both entities, with state anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity and bias-motivated sentencing enhancements including in Brčko itself, and no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or gender expression. No documented local regime of arrests, facility bans or border document targeting distinguishes it, and no recurring local attacks on transgender visitors are known. National social attitudes remain strongly hostile toward homosexuality and gender diversity, police protection has failed in past pride-related violence elsewhere, and monitoring reports a worsening climate. In a small district, discovery would be highly visible, with limited specialist support or recourse, though the neutral administration is less aligned with entity-level conservative campaigns.

regions.name: Belize
regions.basis: Belize has no criminal penalty for same-sex conduct or transgender identity after the Supreme Court struck down Section 53 in 2016, a ruling upheld in 2019, and the 2024 Anti-Sexual Harassment Act names gender identity, though the bias-motivation sentencing provision names only sexual orientation. An Immigration Act prohibition remains on the books but Belize states it applies only to commercial sex, and the Caribbean Court of Justice barred blanket exclusion of regional homosexual visitors. Social acceptance is mixed and dated, with substantial religious opposition and past threats against activists, while tourist centres serving foreign visitors are generally more tolerant and everyday enforcement against visitors is not documented. Rural and strongly religious communities may be less accepting. No transgender-specific border, facility, detention, or care restrictions are documented.

regions.name: Cayo
regions.basis: Cayo is Belize's western inland district, centred on San Ignacio and Belmopan, with rural towns, tourist sites and socially conservative Mennonite communities. Nationally, same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016 and upheld in 2019, the 2024 Anti-Sexual Harassment Act names gender identity, and an immigration provision listing homosexuals was narrowed by Caribbean Court of Justice obligations and Belize's stated interpretation. No trans-specific criminal offence, facility restriction or custody rule is documented. Acceptance remains mixed, with organised religious opposition alongside growing LGBT visibility. In Cayo, fewer urban LGBT organisations, clinics and visitor services than in Belize City or coastal resorts may mean less local support and more staring or moral disapproval, particularly outside tourist areas, while no distinct local law changes the national position.

regions.name: Stann Creek
regions.basis: Stann Creek is a small coastal town in southern Belize, where trans visitors encounter the national regime: consensual same-sex conduct is decriminalised following the 2016 Supreme Court ruling upheld in 2019, the 2024 Anti-Sexual Harassment Act names gender identity, and bias-motivated sentencing covers sexual orientation, though gender identity is not named there. Immigration law retains an older prohibited-immigrant category, but the Caribbean Court of Justice clarified it cannot be applied as a blanket ban on homosexual CARICOM nationals. No region-specific information distinguishes Stann Creek from the national picture on border practices, facilities, policing, health care, or social reaction, and no local trans-specific targeting or protective exception is known.

regions.name: Chuquisaca
regions.basis: Bolivia does not criminalise same-sex activity and its constitution and Law 045 prohibit discrimination based on gender identity, with gender-identity motivation as an aggravating factor. The 2016 Gender Identity Law allows adults to change name, sex and photograph on documents through a confidential administrative procedure. Enforcement is weak: the Ombudsman found few investigations and no sentences for murders of LGBT people in 2017, and a 2024 survey documented widespread exclusion, although polling shows majority support for equal rights for transgender people. No region-specific information distinguishes Chuquisaca, including Sucre, from the national picture on border, facility, policing or violence practice affecting visitors.

regions.name: Saint Andrew
regions.basis: Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2022 following a constitutional challenge, but has no recognised same-sex relationships and its 2020 employment anti-discrimination law does not list gender identity or expression as protected grounds. A documented 2018 attack on a trans activist resulted in conviction with a BDS$460 fine or three months in prison and no jail time imposed, illustrating limited accountability for anti-trans violence. Public officials have also questioned LGBT migration and asylum claims. Saint Andrew is a rural inland parish administered under the same national laws and institutions as the rest of Barbados, with no separate parish-level rules, policing, or protections documented to distinguish a transgender visitor's treatment there from the national picture.

regions.name: Saint George
regions.basis: Saint George contains Bridgetown, Barbados's capital and main commercial, port and tourist centre, so a transgender visitor is more likely to encounter urban anonymity, foreign-visitor infrastructure, hotels and services accustomed to outsiders, and police and hospitals operating under national law than in a small rural community where recognition and gossip travel quickly. The inherited national regime remains decisive after discovery: same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2022, but there is no documented distinct protection for transgender visitors, employment law does not list gender identity or expression, and a 2018 serious attack resulted in only a nominal fine, indicating weak recourse. No local rule changes that picture.

regions.name: Saint John
regions.basis: Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2022 following a constitutional challenge, but employment protection does not list gender identity or expression, and a 2018 attack on a trans activist resulted in a conviction with only a small fine and no jail time, illustrating limited recourse. Saint John is a largely residential and rural parish without a distinct border, detention, or facility regime from the national system; no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture. Enforcement and social attitudes are governed nationally, with everyday interaction likely shaped by general Barbadian tolerance tempered by conservatism.

regions.name: Saint Joseph
regions.basis: Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct between men in 2022 following a constitutional challenge brought by trans activist Alexa Hoffmann, and its courts have found sexual-orientation discrimination unconstitutional. However employment discrimination law does not list gender identity or expression, and a serious 2018 cleaver attack on Hoffmann resulted in a small fine rather than jail, signalling limited recourse for anti-trans violence. No same-sex union is recognised. Saint Joseph is a rural northern parish with no documented separate entry, facility, policing or healthcare regime for trans visitors; no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of trans visitors from the national picture, and everyday exposure would therefore follow national law and broader Barbadian social attitudes.

regions.name: Saint Lucy
regions.basis: Saint Lucy is a largely rural, agricultural parish in eastern Barbados, distant from Bridgetown's tourist and service centre and with a close-knit, socially conservative community where a visibly transgender visitor is more conspicuous and has less access to legal aid, shelters or LGBTQ support. It operates under Barbados's national regime: same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2022, but gender identity is not expressly protected in employment law and a serious 2018 attack on a trans activist resulted in a trivial financial penalty rather than jail. No parish-level protective measures or documented exceptions distinguish Saint Lucy from the national picture, while rural isolation may reduce everyday scrutiny but also reduce recourse if harassment or a police encounter occurs.

regions.name: Saint Michael
regions.basis: Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2022 after a constitutional challenge brought by trans activist Alexa Hoffmann, and courts have shown willingness to strike discriminatory law. There is no documented trans-specific criminal offence, facility ban, or police targeting of visitors, but employment protection omits gender identity, no same-sex relationship recognition exists, and a 2018 meat-cleaver attack on Hoffmann resulted in conviction with only a small fine, indicating weak accountability. Saint Michael contains Bridgetown, the capital, and is the island's dense urban and tourist centre, where anonymity, visitor services and greater social tolerance than rural parishes reduce everyday friction, though national law, policing and social conservatism apply unchanged.

regions.name: Saint Peter
regions.basis: Saint Peter, a parish on Barbados's northern west coast centred on Speightstown, inherits the national regime for a transgender visitor conditional on discovery. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised nationally in December 2022 following a constitutional challenge brought by trans activist Alexa Hoffmann, but employment anti-discrimination law omits gender identity and expression, no same-sex union recognition exists, and the state does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category. A serious 2018 attack on Hoffmann led in 2019 to conviction with only a small fine, no imprisonment, showing limited recourse for trans-specific violence. Tourism, common-law institutions and English-speaking visitor infrastructure are national features, and no region-specific information distinguishes Saint Peter from the national picture for a trans visitor once outed.

regions.name: Saint Philip
regions.basis: Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct between men in December 2022 after a constitutional challenge, and its High Court found sexual-orientation discrimination unconstitutional. Employment protection from 2020 covers sex and sexual orientation but not gender identity or expression, and no same-sex relationship recognition is in place. A 2018 attack on trans activist Alexa Hoffmann resulted in conviction but only a small fine, showing limited accountability for anti-trans violence. The government has questioned LGBT asylum migration and does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a category. Saint Philip, an eastern parish, has no region-specific information distinguishing its treatment of trans visitors from the national picture.

regions.name: Saint Thomas
regions.basis: Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2022 following a constitutional challenge brought by a trans claimant, and its courts have recognised sexual-orientation discrimination as unconstitutional, but employment protections do not expressly cover gender identity, same-sex relationships are unrecognised, and a documented 2018 attack on a trans activist resulted in only a small fine with no jail time. Saint Thomas is a rural inland parish with no separate legal regime, LGBT venues, or documented local exceptions, and as a small island its policing, courts, and social norms operate under the same national framework as the rest of Barbados, with a close-knit, church-going community and little tourist-facing infrastructure compared with Bridgetown and the west and south coasts.

regions.name: Belait
regions.basis: Belait, a district centred on Kuala Belait and Seria, operates under Brunei's national Syariah Penal Code Order, which criminalises a man dressing as a woman or a woman dressing as a man without reasonable excuse or for immoral purposes, with documented enforcement including a 2015 fine and default imprisonment for cross-dressing in a public place. Travellers cannot align documents with presentation because Brunei does not permit name or gender-marker changes and does not permit sex reassignment surgery. Same-sex conduct carries severe penalties, including death by stoning under stringent evidentiary conditions, currently subject to a revocable moratorium in force since 2019, and imprisonment and caning where that threshold is not met. No region-specific information distinguishes Belait from the national picture on enforcement or protections.

regions.name: Brunei-Muara
regions.basis: Brunei-Muara is the capital district, centred on Bandar Seri Begawan, where government offices, major hotels and Syariah enforcement are concentrated and where a cross-dressing detention and conviction were documented. The district operates under Brunei's national Syariah Penal Code, which criminalises dressing as another sex without reasonable excuse and provides severe penalties for same-sex conduct, with capital provisions subject to a revocable moratorium. There is no local exception, document-alignment process or protective regime for visitors. Urban concentration may increase official encounters, while no district-specific tolerance offsets the enforced national restrictions.

regions.name: Temburong
regions.basis: Temburong is Brunei's easternmost district, largely rural and separated from the capital by Malaysian Sarawak, with small, predominantly Malay Muslim communities, limited tourism and few medical or legal facilities. The national Syariah Penal Code criminalises cross-dressing or posing as a different sex, with documented fines and imprisonment, and does not permit changing name or gender on official documents. Same-sex penalties include stoning de jure, currently held under a revocable death-penalty moratorium, with whipping and imprisonment applied instead. No local exception or protective regime distinguishes Temburong; its remoteness and close-knit visibility increase scrutiny and reduce access to embassies, hospitals and legal help if a visitor is outed.

regions.name: Tutong
regions.basis: Tutong is a largely rural, Malay-Muslim coastal district in western Brunei centred on the small town of Tutong, with limited tourism, limited anonymity, and a socially conservative community. It is governed by the same national Syariah Penal Code as the rest of Brunei, including criminalisation of cross-gender dressing and severe penalties for same-sex conduct, with a death-penalty moratorium that remains revocable. Gender markers and names cannot be changed and sex reassignment is not permitted, so a visitor cannot make documents match presentation. No local exception, protective service or more tolerant enclave is known; in a small town, discovery is more likely to be reported locally and there is little independent recourse.

regions.name: Bumthang
regions.basis: Bumthang, in Bhutan's central Jakar valley, inherits the national regime: consensual same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021, but there is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no legal gender recognition, and administrative marker changes are suspended. Reported practice provides little recourse if a visitor is outed, with trans people more than four times as likely to face assault, police dismissing complaints by reference to a male identity marker, and referrals moving slowly. Health-care discrimination is also documented nationally. Bumthang is rural and traditionally conservative, with less anonymity and visitor-facing support than Thimphu or Paro and no distinct local protective law.

regions.name: Chukha
regions.basis: Chukha, on Bhutan's southern border, operates under the same national framework as the rest of the country, with no region-specific information distinguishing it from the national picture. Consensual same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021, but Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law protecting gender identity and no legal gender recognition, and gender markers cannot be changed through a standardised process. Trans people are reported to be more than four times as likely to face assault, police have dismissed complaints where identity cards record a male marker, and supportive health-care guidance coexists with reports of people being turned away. For a visitor, discovery therefore carries risks of police non-response, impunity, and service denial rather than criminalisation for identity.

regions.name: Dagana
regions.basis: Dagana in southern Bhutan operates under the same national framework as the rest of the country: consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2021 and no trans-specific criminal offence is documented, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and administrative marker changes are suspended. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation could face questioning, and documented reporting of assaults against trans people shows police may dismiss complaints when identity documents record a male marker, with families and committee referrals offering slow recourse. Health-care access is also documented as uneven. No region-specific information distinguishes Dagana from the national picture on enforcement, tolerance, tourism exposure or available recourse.

regions.name: Gasa
regions.basis: Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021 and has no criminal penalty for transgender identity or presentation, but provides no anti-discrimination protection and no legal gender recognition, and in practice police have dismissed trans people's assault complaints by reference to male identity-card markers, leaving violence largely unpunished and health care uneven. Gasa is a remote, high-altitude northern district centred on Gasa town, reached mainly through trekking routes, with sparse hospitals, limited police and legal-aid capacity, and close-knit traditional communities far from Thimphu-based support organisations. No local protective exception is known; a visitor recognised as trans there would face similar impunity and service denial, magnified by distance from referral networks and medical care.

regions.name: Haa
regions.basis: Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021, ending prior unnatural-sex provisions, but provides no stand-alone anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and offers no legal gender recognition, with administrative marker changes suspended. Trans people face documented stigma and discrimination, particularly in health care, and are reported to experience assault at well above general-population rates, with police treating complaints from people whose identity cards record a male marker as violence between men and referrals moving slowly, producing impunity. Official medical and gender-based-violence guidance calls for sensitive care. No region-specific information distinguishes Haa from the national picture.

regions.name: Lhuntse
regions.basis: Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021, but provides no stand-alone anti-discrimination protection for gender identity and no legal gender recognition, with marker changes suspended for lack of guidelines. Trans people face documented stigma and healthcare turnaway, and police have dismissed complaints about assault by treating identity documents recording a male marker as violence between men, leaving impunity. Official health procedures call for gender-sensitive care, yet referrals are slow and no relationship recognition exists for a partner. No region-specific information distinguishes Lhuntse from the national picture; no separate local law, services, or enforcement pattern is documented.

regions.name: Mongar
regions.basis: Mongar is a remote eastern district of Bhutan, a largely rural, hill-based area with limited tourist infrastructure, fewer specialist health services and greater distance from Thimphu-based support organisations and legal assistance than the capital. Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021, but has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no legal gender recognition, and suspended marker changes. Reported assault risk for trans people is elevated, police complaints are often dismissed by reference to male identity-card markers, and referrals move slowly, creating impunity. Health-care denial is also reported. In Mongar, lower anonymity, traditional community ties and sparse local recourse can magnify exposure after discovery, with no distinct local protection.

regions.name: Paro
regions.basis: Paro is Bhutan's main international gateway and a concentrated centre for hotels, airport services and visitors travelling onward to Thimphu, so a transgender visitor is most likely to be encountered there through passport and hotel document checks rather than in a separate local legal system. Bhutan repealed its unenforced same-sex provisions in 2021 but has no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, no legal gender recognition and no partner recognition, and national reporting describes police dismissing trans complainants because identity cards carry a male marker, leaving assaults largely unremedied and health care uneven. Paro's tourist-facing setting may offer greater anonymity and staff familiarity with foreigners than remote districts, but it also concentrates formal identification, with no documented Paro-specific protection or targeting beyond the national framework.

regions.name: Pemagatshel
regions.basis: Pemagatshel is a remote, rural eastern district of Bhutan, far from Thimphu and main tourist routes, with small, closely knit Sharchop communities and limited hospitals, legal aid and LGBTQ support services. Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021 and imposes no entry ban, facility rule or criminal penalty for being transgender, but provides no anti-discrimination protection or legal gender recognition, and police have dismissed trans women's complaints by treating them as violence between men. In Pemagatshel, that impunity, distance from referral services, and greater local visibility mean a trans visitor who is outed faces stigma, possible assault with little recourse, and poor continuity of care, with help likely distant and slow.

regions.name: Punakha
regions.basis: Punakha, a former capital and major stop on Bhutan's main tourist circuit in the Punakha-Wangdue valley, encounters foreign visitors regularly in hotels, dzongs and sites along the Thimphu-Paro route, so foreign presence itself is familiar. That familiarity does not change the national regime: consensual same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021, but Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, no legal gender recognition, and no pattern of police redress for anti-trans violence, with complaints documented as dismissed when identity cards carry a male marker. Health-care discrimination and stigma persist despite official sensitive-care guidance. No Punakha-specific law or enforcement practice distinguishes it from the national picture.

regions.name: Samdrup Jongkhar
regions.basis: Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021, but has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law covering gender identity and no legal gender recognition, with administrative marker changes suspended. Trans people are reported to face markedly higher assault rates, and police have dismissed complaints by treating violence against a trans woman as violence between men because her identity card carries a male marker, with slow referrals and impunity. Healthcare discrimination is documented despite professional guidance requiring sensitive care. No region-specific information distinguishes Samdrup Jongkhar, in Bhutan's southeast, from the national picture on visitor-facing law, policing, or services, so a visitor there would encounter that national regime.

regions.name: Samtse
regions.basis: Samtse is a southwestern border district of Bhutan where a transgender visitor conditional on discovery faces the national regime: consensual same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 but there are no explicit anti-discrimination protections for sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and no legal gender recognition, with administrative marker changes suspended. Trans people face elevated assault risk and police may dismiss complaints when identity documents show a male marker, with slow referrals and impunity, while health care remains a setting where they are turned away or poorly served despite official guidance requiring gender-identity-sensitive care. No region-specific information distinguishes Samtse from the national picture on visitor treatment, policing, or services.

regions.name: Sarpang
regions.basis: Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021, but provides no stand-alone anti-discrimination protection for gender identity and no legal gender recognition, with administrative marker changes suspended. Trans people face elevated assault risk, and police have dismissed complaints where identity documents carry a male marker, treating violence as between men, creating impunity and slow referrals. Discrimination persists in health care despite official guidance for gender-identity-sensitive care. No region-specific information distinguishes Sarpang from the national picture, so its conditions reflect the same legal framework and enforcement practice.

regions.name: Thimpu
regions.basis: Thimpu, as Bhutan's capital, concentrates tourism, hotels, hospitals and the LGBTQIA+ organisations and referral networks described nationally, offering greater anonymity than rural areas and readier access to visitor infrastructure, but operates under the same national regime. Consensual same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, yet there is no anti-discrimination protection, no legal gender recognition, and gender-marker changes are suspended. Trans people report assault at elevated rates, police dismissal of complaints when identity cards carry a male marker, slow referrals and impunity, and discrimination including in health care. A visitor who is outed therefore faces stigma, service friction and weak recourse rather than imprisonment, with Thimpu's urban setting providing only modest mitigation.

regions.name: Trashigang
regions.basis: Trashigang is a remote eastern district of Bhutan where national law applies without a separate local regime for transgender visitors. Consensual same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021, but there is no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, no legal gender recognition, and no legal recognition for a partner read as same-sex. Trans people report assault at more than four times the general rate, police dismissing complaints when identity documents show a male marker, and being turned away or poorly served in health care despite official guidance for gender-sensitive care. No region-specific information distinguishes Trashigang’s treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture, beyond its rural character and limited services.

regions.name: Trashiyangtse
regions.basis: Trashiyangtse is a small, remote district town in eastern Bhutan with limited tourist infrastructure, fewer health and legal services than Thimphu or Paro, and a close-knit, socially conservative community where anonymity is low. Bhutan has not criminalised consensual same-sex intimacy since 2021 and has no trans-specific offence, but there is no anti-discrimination protection or legal gender recognition, and administrative marker changes are suspended. Police have been reported to dismiss violence against trans people by treating complaints as between men because identity cards record a male marker, leaving impunity. Health care is a setting where trans people report being turned away despite formal guidance for gender-sensitive care. No distinct local law or protective service alters this national picture, and distance from national support networks makes recourse thinner if a visitor is outed.

regions.name: Trongsa
regions.basis: Trongsa is a small, rural administrative town in central Bhutan with limited specialist health, legal and community services, and no local protective infrastructure distinct from the national system. Bhutan removed its same-sex conduct provisions in 2021 and imposes no trans-specific criminal offence, but provides no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity and no legal gender recognition. Police have dismissed assault complaints by trans people because identity cards show a male marker, leaving violence effectively unaddressed, and trans people report being turned away or poorly served in health care despite official guidance for gender-identity-sensitive care. Distance from Thimphu-based support organisations makes remedies harder to pursue from Trongsa. A travelling partner would receive no legal recognition.

regions.name: Tsirang
regions.basis: A transgender visitor in Tsirang faces Bhutan's national position: consensual same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021, with no reversal, and there is no trans-specific criminal offence, organised targeting, or documented border or facility exclusion for visitors. There is also no stand-alone anti-discrimination protection, police have dismissed complaints by treating a trans woman with a male-marked identity card as a victim of violence between men, and trans people are reported to face higher assault risk with practical impunity and discrimination in health care, despite official guidance requiring sensitive care. No region-specific information distinguishes Tsirang from the national picture.

regions.name: Wangdue Phodrang
regions.basis: Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021 after the unnatural sex provisions had gone unenforced for at least fifteen years, but created no protective framework, with no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity and no legal gender recognition available to residents. Trans people are reported to face markedly higher assault rates, with police dismissing complaints when identity documents record a male marker and families discouraging reporting, producing impunity. Health care access is also constrained despite official guidance requiring gender-identity-sensitive care. No region-specific information distinguishes Wangdue Phodrang from the national picture.

regions.name: Zhemgang
regions.basis: Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021, removing imprisonment provisions that had gone unenforced for many years, but created no protective framework for transgender visitors. There is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, legal gender recognition is unavailable and marker changes are suspended, and health-care access remains a setting where trans people can be turned away. Police practice is a central risk: complaints can be dismissed because identity documents record a male marker, with violence treated as between two men and referrals moving slowly, producing impunity despite a reported assault rate more than four times the general population. No region-specific information distinguishes Zhemgang from the national picture.

regions.name: Central District
regions.basis: Botswana law provides no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct after the High Court's 2019 ruling, upheld on appeal in 2021, and the 2026 deletion of the former provisions, with prosecutions previously rare and police not documented as targeting same-sex activity. Court rulings in 2017 required recognition of transgender people's gender identity on identity documents, although no clear administrative process has been established. Documented violence against transgender people is absent rather than shown to be high, tolerance measures have risen, and official statements have been mixed. For Central District, no region-specific information distinguishes its legal or enforcement conditions from the national picture.

regions.name: Ghanzi District
regions.basis: Botswana has no documented trans-specific criminal offence, and consensual same-sex conduct is lawful following the 2019 High Court decision, upheld on appeal in 2021 and formally removed from the Penal Code in 2026. Court rulings in 2017 required recognition of two transgender citizens' gender identities, although no clear administrative gender-marker process had been introduced by 2023. Employment law prohibits sexual-orientation discrimination, but same-sex partnerships are not recognised. Societal discrimination persists despite rising tolerance, while documented violence against trans people is absent from the available record and police have not been shown to target same-sex activity. No region-specific information distinguishes Ghanzi District from the national picture for a transgender visitor.

regions.name: Kgatleng District
regions.basis: Kgatleng District, centred on Mochudi in the Bakgatla traditional area north-east of Gaborone, is largely rural and peri-urban, with low tourism and less urban anonymity than the capital. Botswana law since 2019, upheld on appeal in 2021, does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct, and courts have recognised gender identity in individual document cases, though no clear administrative gender-recognition process exists. Nationally, violence specifically targeting trans people is not documented, police have not been documented targeting same-sex activity, and tolerance has risen, alongside persistent societal discrimination and mixed official rhetoric. In Kgatleng, traditional community structures and a more conservative rural setting make curiosity, staring and disapproval more likely, with fewer visitor-facing services locally, while proximity to Gaborone provides access to national institutions; no district-level hostile law or targeted enforcement is known.

regions.name: Kweneng District
regions.basis: Kweneng District is a largely rural, Setswana-majority district in central Botswana where national law applies without a separate local regime. Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful following High Court and Court of Appeal decisions, and courts have ordered recognition of gender identity on identity documents in individual cases, though no clear administrative process for marker change has been introduced. There is no documented pattern of police targeting transgender visitors, trans-specific violence, or entry restrictions based on gender identity, and a registered LGBTIQ+ organisation provides community and legal support nationally. Social attitudes remain mixed, with growing stated tolerance alongside conservative opinion, so a visitor who is outed may face staring, curiosity or disapproval, particularly in smaller communities, but not criminalisation or state detention for being transgender. No region-specific information distinguishes conditions here from the national picture.

regions.name: North-East District
regions.basis: North-East District is centred on Francistown, Botswana's second city and a commercial, transport and border hub with a comparatively urban and internationally mixed population serving foreign visitors through hotels, clinics and transport services. It shares the national legal framework: consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by the courts in 2019 and 2021 and removed from the statute book in 2026, courts have recognised residents' gender identity, employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited, and LEGABIBO is legally established. No distinct local law, police practice or pattern of violence against transgender visitors is known for the district. Societal discrimination persists nationally, formal anti-discrimination coverage for gender identity remains incomplete, and partnership recognition is unavailable, while urban Francistown is generally more accustomed to diverse visitors than rural areas.

regions.name: North-West District
regions.basis: Botswana has no criminal offence covering transgender identity or expression, and consensual same-sex conduct was upheld as lawful by the Court of Appeal in 2021, with the relevant Penal Code paragraphs formally deleted in 2026. High Court rulings in 2017 required recognition of transgender people's gender identity on identity documents, although no clear administrative process for legal gender recognition had been introduced by 2023. No documented pattern of violence against transgender visitors is recorded, while societal discrimination has been reported and tolerance measures remain divided. LEGABIBO is legally registered and provides support resources. No region-specific information distinguishes North-West District from the national picture.

regions.name: Southern District
regions.basis: Botswana decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct through court rulings in 2019 and 2021, with the relevant Penal Code provisions formally removed in 2026, and police targeting of same-sex activity has not been documented. Transgender people have won court recognition of gender identity, although administrative procedures remain unsettled, and employment law prohibits sexual-orientation discrimination, but same-sex partnerships receive no marriage or spousal recognition. Social tolerance has risen to about half of respondents, alongside recorded societal discrimination and mixed official statements. No region-specific information distinguishes Southern District from the national picture, so the same national legal framework, community organisations, and social attitudes apply there.

regions.name: Basse-Kotto
regions.basis: Basse-Kotto offers no region-specific information that distinguishes it from the national picture for a transgender visitor. Private same-sex activity is legal, but public same-sex affection is punishable by six months to two years' imprisonment or a fine, and no legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection, or documented trans-specific border, facilities, custody, or care safeguards exist. Officials assess visitors against home-issued documents. Societal discrimination is entrenched, LGBTQ people conceal their identities, and domestic organisations have documented false-accusation arrests and mistreatment by law enforcement. If outed, a visitor could face arrest, detention, extortion or abuse with no established recourse, while other risks remain undocumented rather than absent.

regions.name: Kémo
regions.basis: Kémo offers no region-specific information distinguishing it from the national picture in the Central African Republic, so assessment rests on that national regime. Private same-sex activity is legal, but public same-sex affection is punishable by six months to two years' imprisonment or a fine, with heavier penalties where a child is involved. There is no legal gender recognition, no prohibition of discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity in health, employment, education or services, and marriage is constitutionally limited to a man and a woman. Domestic advocacy has documented arrests on false accusations and mistreatment including torture by law enforcement, while discussion of gender identity is taboo and framed as foreign, leaving trans visitors reliant on concealment with little recourse if discovered.

regions.name: Lobaye
regions.basis: Lobaye in southwestern Central African Republic is a sparsely populated, largely rural prefecture bordering Congo and Cameroon, centred on small towns such as Mbaiki, with limited health, legal and visitor infrastructure and a weak day-to-day state presence amid ongoing armed-group insecurity nationally. It inherits the national regime: public same-sex affection is punishable by imprisonment, police mistreatment of LGBTQ people is documented, there is no anti-discrimination protection or legal gender recognition, and societal discrimination is entrenched and taboo. A trans visitor outed there would be judged against home documents, with no local recourse, and would face heightened visibility and hostility in close-knit communities and limited care or consular support.

regions.name: Mambéré-Kadéï
regions.basis: Transgender visitors in Mambéré-Kadéï face the Central African Republic's national framework, with no region-specific information distinguishing the prefecture from the national picture. Private same-sex conduct is legal, but public expression of same-sex affection is punishable by imprisonment or fines, and a domestic organisation has documented arrests following false accusations and mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement. Legal gender recognition does not exist, officials assess visitors against documents as issued, and no law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Societal discrimination is entrenched, discussion of gender identity is taboo, and LGBTQ people commonly conceal their identities to avoid discrimination, blackmail and other harm, with no known organisations promoting LGBTQ rights.

regions.name: Nana-Mambéré
regions.basis: In the Central African Republic, public expression of same-sex affection is punishable by six months to two years' imprisonment or a fine, no legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection exists, and domestic organisations have documented arrests, mistreatment and torture by law enforcement, with sexual orientation and gender identity widely taboo and attributed to foreign influence. Nana-Mambéré, centred on Bossangoa in the remote north-west, is largely rural and conflict-affected, with sparse state services, limited medical and consular recourse, armed insecurity and virtually no tourism infrastructure. No local trans-specific protections or exceptions are known. A visitor who is outed would face the national legal exposure in a place where institutions are weaker, visibility is higher, and assistance is distant.

regions.name: Ouaka
regions.basis: Ouaka is a largely rural central prefecture centred on Bambari, with no separate prefectural legal regime, no documented transgender community infrastructure, protections or local tolerance distinguishing it from the national picture. The national law criminalising public same-sex affection with imprisonment, combined with entrenched societal discrimination, taboo around sexual orientation and gender identity, absence of anti-discrimination protection and of legal gender recognition, and documented mistreatment of LGBTQ people by law enforcement with no known advocacy organisations or reliable recourse, applies fully there. In smaller communities visibility and concealment pressures are greater and institutional protection is thin, so a visitor who is outed faces entrenched hostility and police risk with little practical remedy.

regions.name: Ouham
regions.basis: Ouham is a largely rural prefecture in north-western Central African Republic centred on Bossangoa, with sparse public services, weak institutional presence outside main towns, and a history of armed-group violence and displacement that leaves little effective protection or recourse. Private same-sex conduct is legal, but public same-sex affection is punishable by imprisonment under Article 85, same-sex relationships have no recognition, and there is no legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection. Sexual orientation and gender identity are taboo, widely rejected as foreign, and transgender people face entrenched societal discrimination and concealment; national reporting documents police mistreatment of LGBTQ people. No Ouham-specific tolerance or protective exceptions are known.

regions.name: Ouham-Pendé
regions.basis: Ouham-Pendé, centred on Bossangoa in the north-west, is governed for a transgender visitor by the same national framework as the rest of the Central African Republic: private same-sex conduct is legal but public same-sex affection is punishable by six months to two years' imprisonment or a fine, no legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection exists, and foreign documents are assessed as issued. Discrimination is described as entrenched and the subject taboo, with concealment common, while domestic monitoring has documented arrests on false accusations and mistreatment by law enforcement, and no known LGBTQ rights organisations operate nationally. No region-specific information distinguishes Ouham-Pendé from the national picture on trans-specific enforcement, facilities, custody, care, or official protection.

regions.name: Sangha-Mbaéré
regions.basis: Transgender visitors in Sangha-Mbaéré fall under the national regime of the Central African Republic. Private same-sex activity between consenting adults is legal, but public expression of same-sex affection is punishable by six months to two years' imprisonment or a fine, with heavier penalties where a child is involved. There is no legal gender recognition, no law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in health, employment, education or services, and no transgender-specific protection in documents, facilities, custody or care.
