regions.basis: Sughd inherits Tajikistan's national regime, in which consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 1998 but there is no prohibition of discrimination on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds. Police maintain a register of LGBTIQ people, lure people into fake meetings to register them, harvest contacts and extort money, and conduct raids involving forced HIV testing, arbitrary charges, ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion, with more than ten such police cases documented specifically in Sughd province. Changing documents requires a transsexualism diagnosis and, for transgender women, surgery via an unregulated psychiatric commission, with only three to six people recorded as having changed legal gender, and gender-affirming care is unavailable. Public attitudes are described as entirely negative, senior religious and political figures are openly hostile, and activists operate anonymously without state access. No region-specific protective exception distinguishes Sughd, including Khujent, from the national picture.

regions.name: Ahai
regions.basis: Ahai, centred on Ashgabat, operates under Turkmenistan's national regime, which criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under Article 135, with imprisonment and possible labour-camp sentences, increased penalties for repeat convictions, and provisions retained and strengthened in the 2022 Criminal Code. Trans people are unacknowledged in law, with no gender-recognition mechanism and no anti-discrimination legislation, and the government has framed deviation from traditional norms as a threat to society. Enforcement has involved torture and humiliating interrogation during investigation, confinement to mental hospitals, and vigilante attacks, particularly in prison, alongside impunity for security-service abuses. A trans visitor whose documents record birth sex could be brought within Article 135 through how authorities read their status or relationships. No region-specific information distinguishes Ahai from the national picture.

regions.name: Aileu
regions.basis: Aileu inherits Timor-Leste's national position: same-sex conduct is not criminalised, there is no anti-trans statute, police targeting, or facility ban, health policy must be non-discriminatory on gender identity, and 2024 child-protection and gender-based-violence instruments name transgender people, although hate-crime and general anti-discrimination law do not cover gender identity and reported practice includes verbal abuse and discrimination in public services, with violence mainly family and community based. Locally, Aileu is a largely rural, poor, predominantly Catholic inland municipality near Dili with basic services, little tourism or visible transgender or LGBTI infrastructure, and conservative community norms. A visitor has no local recourse infrastructure and would depend on distant Dili-based services if outed or harassed.

regions.name: Ainaro
regions.basis: Ainaro, a rural and mountainous municipality in south-central Timor-Leste, operates under the same national regime as the rest of the country: same-sex conduct is not criminalised, there is no anti-trans statute or documented police targeting, and a visitor's home passport governs their documents, with no local marker process. Health and child-protection rules formally prohibit discrimination based on gender identity, but hate-crime and general anti-discrimination cover does not extend to gender identity, and reported practice includes verbal abuse and discrimination in services. Family and community violence, rather than state action, is the documented pattern nationally. In Ainaro, visibility and dedicated support are far more limited than in Dili, services are distant, and conservative community norms make recourse harder, while no separate local law or enforcement practice is known.

regions.name: Baucau
regions.basis: Baucau, on Timor-Leste's north coast, operates under the same national regime as the rest of the country: same-sex conduct is not criminalised, there is no trans-specific offence or documented police targeting, and health policy formally bars gender-identity discrimination, though hate-crime and general anti-discrimination protections do not cover gender identity and reported discrimination in public services, including health care, is documented nationally. Violence is described as family and community based rather than state directed. Locally, Baucau is a smaller, more socially conservative and largely rural-centred community than Dili, with less visible LGBT organisation, fewer support services and less frequent public endorsement of diversity, increasing everyday friction and reducing practical recourse if a visitor is outed, while state detention or facility bans are not documented locally.

regions.name: Bobonaro
regions.basis: Bobonaro, in western Timor-Leste near the Indonesian border, inherits the national position: same-sex conduct is not criminalised, no law bars transgender people from facilities or care, health policy must be non-discriminatory on gender identity, and 2024 protection decrees name transgender and non-binary people, though hate-crime and general anti-discrimination law do not cover gender identity and no domestic gender-marker procedure exists for visitors. Locally, Bobonaro is a rural municipality distant from Dili, with fewer health, legal-aid and protective services, a more socially conservative setting, and documented family and community abuse, ostracism and corrective violence affecting transgender men in the area. Physical abuse by authorities is uncommon nationally, but recourse in rural Bobonaro would depend on distant institutions and may be slower for a short-stay visitor.

regions.name: Cova Lima
regions.basis: Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex conduct and has no documented anti-trans statute, arrest pattern, police targeting, or bar on trans visitors using public facilities, health care or employment; a visitor relies on home-issued documents and marker. Health policy must be non-discriminatory on gender identity, and 2024 protection instruments name transgender people and bar disclosure of gender identity without authorisation, yet hate-crime and general anti-discrimination law do not cover gender identity and no enforcement in a trans person's case is documented. Violence is documented as family and community-based, including harassment, bullying and abuse, with reported discrimination in some public services. No region-specific information distinguishes Cova Lima from the national picture.

regions.name: Dili
regions.basis: Dili, the capital, inherits Timor-Leste's non-criminalisation of same-sex conduct and absence of any trans-specific statute, police targeting pattern, or facility or health-care bar, with 2024 protection decrees naming transgender people and prohibiting unauthorised disclosure of gender identity. As the seat of government, hospitals, NGOs and the annual Pride march publicly endorsed by senior officials, Dili offers greater anonymity, foreign presence and institutional access than rural areas, while also documenting family and community abuse, including corrective rape in a Dili study, and verbal abuse and discrimination in public services. Gender-identity hate-crime protection and general anti-discrimination recourse remain absent, and enforcement for trans visitors is not documented.

regions.name: Ermera
regions.basis: Ermera inherits Timor-Leste's non-criminalisation of same-sex conduct and absence of anti-trans statutes, facility bans or police targeting, with the visitor's home passport governing documents and health policy formally prohibiting gender-identity discrimination. Locally, Ermera is a rural, mountainous and strongly Catholic municipality west of Dili with little tourism, no Pride or LGBTQ community infrastructure, and traditional family and church influence. That conservatism, combined with thin police and health services outside Dili and distance from NGOs and legal aid concentrated in the capital, means an outed visitor would face greater family and community rejection, harassment in services, and weaker practical recourse than in Dili, while state imprisonment or organised targeting remains not documented.

regions.name: Lautém
regions.basis: Lautém is Timor-Leste's easternmost, largely rural municipality bordering Indonesia, centred on Lospalos, with little international tourism and limited health and administrative services compared with Dili. Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex conduct, has no anti-trans statute or documented police targeting, and health policy forbids discrimination on gender identity, with 2024 decrees naming transgender people in protection and gender-based-violence services. In practice verbal abuse and discrimination in public services, including medical centres, are reported, and hate-crime coverage does not include gender identity. Violence against transgender people is family and community-based rather than state-directed. In a small, socially conservative, traditional community, a foreign visitor would have less anonymity, fewer urban support networks and more distant recourse, while state enforcement is unlikely to involve arrest or imprisonment for presentation alone.

regions.name: Liquiçá
regions.basis: No region-specific information distinguishes Liquiçá from the national picture for a transgender visitor who is outed. Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex conduct, and there is no documented trans-specific criminal law, facility ban, arrest pattern or police targeting. Health policy formally requires non-discrimination by gender identity, and 2024 protection decrees name transgender people and bar disclosure of identity, but hate-crime and general anti-discrimination law do not cover gender identity. Reporting nationally describes verbal abuse, discrimination in some public services, and family and community violence rather than state-directed abuse, with senior officials having endorsed Pride events in Dili. Practical recourse for identity-based discrimination remains limited.

regions.name: Manatuto
regions.basis: Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex conduct and has no documented anti-trans statute, police targeting, or ban on trans access to facilities, health care or employment, so a trans visitor relies on home-issued documents and faces no domestic marker process. Health policy requires non-discrimination on gender identity, and 2024 protection instruments name transgender and non-binary people, but hate-crime and general anti-discrimination coverage does not extend to gender identity, partnership recognition is closed, and reported practice includes verbal abuse and discrimination in public services, particularly clinics. Documented violence is mainly family and community based, including bullying of transgender students, while senior officials have endorsed Pride in Dili. Manatuto is a more rural, socially conservative eastern municipality than Dili, with fewer tourist services, NGOs and legal or medical support networks, making anonymity lower and practical recourse harder, though no separate local criminal or police regime distinguishes it from national law.

regions.name: Manufahi
regions.basis: Manufahi is a municipality in southern Timor-Leste, with Same as its main town and a largely rural, Portuguese- and Tetum-speaking population. No region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture for a transgender visitor. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised and there is no anti-trans statute, facility ban, or documented police targeting, but gender identity is not covered by hate-crime or general anti-discrimination protection, and legal gender recognition is not available. Health access is formally non-discriminatory, yet reported service discrimination and family and community harassment, including bullying of transgender students, remain documented risks. Visitors rely on home-issued documents, with no domestic marker-change route.

regions.name: Oecusse
regions.basis: Oecusse, Timor-Leste's exclave in West Timor, operates under the same national law: same-sex conduct is not criminalised, there is no anti-trans statute or facility ban, and health policy formally prohibits discrimination on gender identity grounds. Visitors rely on home passports, for which no domestic marker process is documented. Protection is limited, as hate-crime and anti-discrimination law cover sexual orientation but not gender identity, and documented risks are mainly family and community harassment, verbal abuse and discrimination in services rather than state targeting. In this remote, rural exclave far from Dili, limited police, health and legal-aid infrastructure, socially conservative character and cross-border access through Indonesia make local recourse and community support less available than nationally, while no region-specific trans incidents or exceptions are documented.

regions.name: Viqueque
regions.basis: Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex conduct or trans presentation, and national health policy and 2024 protection decrees name gender identity, though hate-crime and general anti-discrimination law do not cover gender identity and reported practice includes verbal abuse and discrimination in public services, with violence mostly family and community based rather than state directed. Viqueque, in the rural east, is largely Catholic, Makasae-speaking and far from Dili's Pride events, NGOs and legal assistance, with limited tourism and thinner medical and police recourse. A visitor there would face greater unfamiliarity, staring and service friction, and fewer practical avenues for complaint or continuity of care, while still encountering no border, facility or custody regime targeting transgender people.

regions.name: 'Eua
regions.basis: Tonga criminalises same-sex activity with up to ten years' imprisonment, although recent enforcement has rarely been documented, and separately penalises a male soliciting in public for an immoral purpose with intent to deceive about true sex, a provision bearing on visible gender presentation. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no recognition of same-sex relationships. Social attitudes are described as fearful and discriminatory, shaped by conservative religious values, and an LGBTQ activist was murdered in 2021. No region-specific information distinguishes 'Eua from the national picture.

regions.name: Ha'apai
regions.basis: Ha'apai is a remote island group in Tonga, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture. Tonga retains a Criminal Offences Act provision criminalising same-sex activity with a maximum of ten years' imprisonment, though recent enforcement is reported as rare or not evidenced, and a separate offence targeting a male soliciting in public with intent to deceive as to his true sex that can bear on visible gender presentation. There is no anti-discrimination protection for visitors in services, and the social climate is described as conservative and hostile, with discrimination and fear affecting fakaleiti and LGBTQ people, including the 2021 murder of an LGBTQ activist.

regions.name: Niuas
regions.basis: Niuas comprises Tonga's small, remote northern islands, far from the capital, with tiny close-knit village populations, sparse services and very little tourism. It shares the national legal regime: same-sex activity remains criminalised with up to ten years' imprisonment though recent enforcement is reported as rare, and a separate public solicitation offence turns on deception about true sex and can bear on visible gender presentation. There is no legal gender recognition, no general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity, and no relationship recognition. Conservatism and religious hostility toward LGBTQ people and fakaleiti are documented nationally. In Niuas, low anonymity and distance from courts and support services increase social exposure if a visitor is recognised, with no local protections documented.

regions.name: Tongatapu
regions.basis: Tongatapu, home to Nuku'alofa and the main international airport and cruise port, inherits Tonga's national regime: same-sex activity remains criminalised on the books with no recent enforcement documented, a public solicitation offence turns on deception about sex, and there is no legal gender recognition or general anti-discrimination protection. As the capital and principal tourist island, it offers more anonymity, foreigner-facing hotels and services, expatriate presence, and a concentrated leiti community than smaller outer islands, but also concentrates police, government institutions and conservative churches, with a national climate of fear and discrimination toward LGBTQ people and fakaleitis. No separate Tongatapu law distinguishes it from the national picture.

regions.name: Vava'u
regions.basis: Vava'u, the northern Tongan island group centred on Neiafu, operates under Tonga's national law, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture. Same-sex activity remains criminalised with up to ten years' imprisonment, though enforcement has been rare in recent years, while a separate offence covers a male soliciting in public for an immoral purpose with intent to deceive as to true sex, bearing on visible gender presentation. There is no legal gender recognition, no route to a Tongan document matching a visitor's gender, and no general prohibition on discrimination based on gender identity. The wider climate is conservative and Christian, with reported fear, discrimination and hostility toward LGBTQ people and fakaleitis, and limited practical recourse if a visitor is outed.

regions.name: Nabeul
regions.basis: Nabeul, on Tunisia's Cap Bon coast with the tourist corridor around Hammamet, inherits a national regime that criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 230 with up to three years' imprisonment and applies the public-decency provision in Article 226 to gender expression, with active arrests, detentions and morality prosecutions documented. Transgender women have been arrested under morality and debauchery provisions and are processed in detention and prison under birth gender and former names, and anal examinations have historically been used as evidence. Hammamet, in Nabeul governorate, was among the locations of the 2024-25 arrests concentrated on gay men and transgender women. No local protective exception, facility-access rule or visitor-specific protection distinguishes Nabeul from the national pattern.

regions.name: Aksaray
regions.basis: Aksaray is a conservative inland province in Central Anatolia on the transit route to Cappadocia, with little international tourism, no visible transgender or LGBTI+ infrastructure, and specialist legal and medical support concentrated in Ankara. If a transgender visitor is identified, Turkish carry-photo-ID requirements at checkpoints enable police stops and General Information Gathering checks, with no comprehensive legal protection on gender identity and no gender-matched detention, segregation and isolation being documented for trans prisoners. Hormone therapy is not publicly covered, so continuity must be arranged privately. The local social environment is traditionally conservative and unfamiliar with gender diversity, offering less anonymity and fewer recourse networks than Istanbul or Ankara, while systematic city-centre policing seen in Istanbul is not documented at the same scale in Aksaray.

regions.name: Antalya
regions.basis: Antalya inherits Turkey's national regime of police identity checks, documented mass detentions and background checks of trans women, segregated prison placement with isolation and ineffective complaints, and no legal protection based on gender identity. Locally, Antalya is a Mediterranean tourism province centred on Antalya city, Alanya, Side and Kaş, where resort businesses, large foreign visitor numbers and Kaş's long-established gay-friendly community create more tolerant everyday attitudes and more discretion toward foreign tourists than in Istanbul or Ankara. That tolerance is limited at checkpoints and hotel registration, where photo identification is routinely required, and it does not change detention or prison conditions if a visitor is outed.

regions.name: Ardahan
regions.basis: Ardahan inherits Turkey's national regime: no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, documented police GBT checks and detentions of trans women, segregation and isolation in prison, and official rhetoric framing LGBT people as a threat to family and children. Locally, Ardahan is a small, rural, socially conservative province in far northeastern Turkey with minimal tourism and no visible LGBT infrastructure, legal-aid networks, or trans community presence. A foreign visitor who is outed would be highly visible, face intense local hostility and curiosity, and have little practical access to lawyers, NGOs, or medical continuity in the province. Distance from Istanbul and Ankara reduces recourse after police detention or discrimination.

regions.name: Artvin
regions.basis: Artvin is a small, mountainous, predominantly conservative Black Sea province on the Georgian border, with small towns and limited tourist infrastructure rather than large-city anonymity. A transgender visitor who is outed there faces the same Turkish regime as nationally: identity checks at transit and border points that can lead to police stops and GBT background checks, no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, and detention in segregation or isolation rather than placement matching identity, with documented ineffective complaints and risks in custody. Locally, distance from major legal-aid and support networks in Istanbul and Ankara, low visibility of transgender people, and close-knit community scrutiny increase exposure and reduce practical recourse, while there is no documented local exception or protective practice to offset the national pattern.

regions.name: Aydın
regions.basis: Aydın is a western Aegean province centred on the city of Aydın and the resort towns of Kuşadası and Didim, where mass tourism and a comparatively liberal coastal public atmosphere make visibly foreign visitors unremarkable in hotels, beaches and promenades. No separate provincial entry, facilities or protective regime applies, so the national framework governs: police identity checks and General Information Gathering detentions, no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, segregation and isolation in prisons, and hormone therapy available only privately at the visitor's cost. Civil-society monitoring includes an Aydın branch of the Human Rights Association. Local tolerance in tourist areas does not change police, custody or proposed criminalisation risks if a visitor is outed.

regions.name: Balıkesir
regions.basis: Balıkesir is a province in western Turkey centred on Balıkesir city, with coastal resorts around Ayvalık, Burhaniye and Edremit and the Kaz Dağları area drawing domestic and some foreign tourists. It inherits Turkey's national regime: no LGBTQ-specific entry ban, but mandatory photo-ID checks, police GBT detentions of trans women, no anti-discrimination protection based on gender identity, segregated prison placement, and no public coverage of hormone therapy. Locally, outside the more visitor-oriented coastal towns, the province is socially conservative with little visible LGBT infrastructure, legal support or affirming healthcare, and a trans visitor is more conspicuous and has less anonymity and recourse than in Istanbul or Izmir, while national stigmatising rhetoric and family-focused campaigns shape official attitudes.

regions.name: Bartın
regions.basis: Turkey's national regime applies in Bartın: police may use identity checks and GBT background checks that have led to street detentions of trans women, prisons segregate trans prisoners in isolation with strip searches and ineffective complaints, there is no comprehensive protection against gender-identity discrimination, and government family and public-morals campaigns stigmatise trans people, while hormone therapy is not publicly covered. Bartın is a small, socially conservative Black Sea province with the coastal tourist town of Amasra, but lacks the anonymity, trans community infrastructure and legal-aid networks of Istanbul. No distinct local law or organised local targeting is documented, so exposure rests mainly on national policing and detention combined with greater local visibility and social disapproval.

regions.name: Batman
regions.basis: Batman is a socially conservative, Kurdish-majority province in southeastern Turkey with low public visibility for LGBT people, few local support organisations and limited access to the metropolitan legal-aid networks concentrated in Istanbul and Ankara. A trans visitor who is identified would face the national pattern of police identity checks, discriminatory rhetoric and segregation in custody, with less local recourse and greater risk of community hostility in a close-knit, conservative setting. Tourism is mainly domestic and centred on sites such as Hasankeyf, so foreign visitors have little established support infrastructure. No Batman-specific enforcement campaign distinguishes the province, but local conservatism and distance from protective institutions compound the national risks.

regions.name: Bayburt
regions.basis: Bayburt inherits Turkey's national regime for a transgender visitor who is discovered: no specific entry ban, but police identity checks can lead to street stops, General Information Gathering background checks and detention, with no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection on gender identity, and detention involving segregation, isolation and ineffective complaints. Locally, Bayburt is a small, rural, socially conservative province in eastern Anatolia with very low tourism and foreign presence, limited anonymity, and no visible transgender community, support organizations or specialized legal aid. That makes a visibly transgender visitor conspicuous, increases likelihood of hostile social reaction and police attention, and reduces practical access to sympathetic lawyers, medical care for continuing hormone therapy, and advocacy support available in larger western cities, while national stigmatizing rhetoric and family-protection enforcement trends shape local official attitudes.

regions.name: Bilecik
regions.basis: Bilecik is a small inland province in northwestern Turkey with a socially conservative environment and no documented local protective exception, tourist-facing tolerance, or dedicated support infrastructure; major-city legal and civil-society assistance is distant. A transgender visitor who is discovered there faces the national regime: discretionary identity checks and General Information Gathering detentions documented in Istanbul in 2025, systematic detention of LGBTI+ people, no comprehensive discrimination protection, official rhetoric framing LGBTI+ people as a threat, and prison segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, with documented custody deaths and ineffective complaints.

regions.name: Bingöl
regions.basis: Bingöl, in eastern Turkey, inherits the national regime: no entry bar for LGBTQ travellers, but police identity checks, documented detentions and GBT recording of trans women, no comprehensive discrimination protection, segregation of trans prisoners, and private payment for hormone care. Locally, Bingöl is a small, predominantly Kurdish, socially conservative and rural province with little trans-specific infrastructure, few lawyers or NGOs able to intervene, limited anonymity in small communities, and a visible security presence. Conditional on being outed, a visitor would face greater social hostility and weaker practical recourse than in Istanbul or Ankara, with hospital and police responses likely shaped by conservative local norms and distance from metropolitan support networks.

regions.name: Bitlis
regions.basis: Bitlis is a small, socially conservative province in eastern Turkey with low tourism, limited anonymity and few LGBT support, legal-aid or health networks, so a foreign transgender visitor who is recognised as trans is highly conspicuous locally. It stands under Turkey-wide conditions: identification must be carried at checks, police have used street stops and General Information Gathering background checks and detention against trans women, there is no comprehensive discrimination or gender-identity protection, and prisons segregate trans prisoners in isolation rather than matching placement, with documented strip searches, restricted healthcare and an uninvestigated death in custody. Hormone therapy is not publicly covered, draft proposals to criminalise LGBT advocacy reflect official hostility, and stereotyped conservative attitudes in a small city leave less practical recourse and greater exposure to harassment or police action than in large metropolitan centres.

regions.name: Bolu
regions.basis: Bolu is an inland, socially conservative province on the Istanbul–Ankara highway with mainly domestic tourism around Abant, Yedigöller and Kartalkaya, and little visible LGBTQ infrastructure or independent legal support compared with Istanbul or Ankara. A transgender visitor outed there faces the same national regime as elsewhere in Turkey: police identity checks and General Information Gathering detention, no anti-discrimination protection based on gender identity, segregation in custody, and heightened state rhetoric around family and public morals, alongside raids on LGBTQ organisations. Locally, conservative attitudes, smaller-city visibility and limited recourse increase social hostility and the practical risk of humiliation, refusal or police escalation, with no documented local exception or protective practice for visitors.

regions.name: Burdur
regions.basis: Burdur is a small, inland province in southwestern Turkey with a socially conservative population, limited tourism compared with coastal resorts, and no known LGBTQ community infrastructure, legal-aid clinic or rights organisation based locally. A transgender visitor would face the national regime: no entry ban for LGBTQ travellers, but photo-ID checks at transit points can initiate police contact, including General Information Gathering checks and documented street detentions, with 313 LGBTI+ violations recorded in 2025 nationally. There is no discrimination protection based on gender identity, official rhetoric frames LGBTQ people as a threat to family and children, prisoners are segregated rather than placed according to gender identity, and hormone therapy is not covered publicly. In Burdur, distance from major-city legal support makes recourse after outing more difficult.

regions.name: Bursa
regions.basis: Bursa inherits Turkey's national regime: no entry bar for LGBTQ visitors, but routine photo-ID checks, police GBT background checks and documented street detentions of trans women, no discrimination protection based on gender identity, segregated and isolation-based prison placement, and state rhetoric framing LGBT people as a threat to family and children. Locally, Bursa is a large but socially conservative inland city with a much smaller and less visible trans and queer scene than Istanbul, few specialist legal-support networks, and no local protective ordinances. Its thermal-hotel and winter-resort tourism brings gender-segregated bathing, hotel registration and police ID checks to many visitors. If outed, a visitor would face the same detention and ineffective-complaint risks nationally, with less community support and greater social hostility locally.

regions.name: Karabük
regions.basis: Karabük inherits Turkey's national regime: no entry bar for LGBTQ visitors, but routine photo-ID checks at checkpoints can initiate police contact, there is no comprehensive protection against discrimination based on gender identity, and trans prisoners are held through segregation and isolation with ineffective complaints and restricted healthcare. Nationally documented GBT detentions of trans women, rising violations, official anti-LGBT rhetoric and recent investigations of support organisations shape risk if a visitor is discovered. Locally, Karabük and Safranbolu are a more conservative provincial area with a small tourist economy, little visible LGBT infrastructure or local legal support, and social attitudes likely less tolerant than in major metropolitan centres.

regions.name: Karaman
regions.basis: Karaman, a small and socially conservative city in central Anatolia, has no distinct entry rule for transgender visitors, so exposure follows the national regime of police identity checks, GBT background checks and detention documented in Istanbul and nationwide, with no comprehensive protection against discrimination on gender identity and segregated prison placement if detained. Locally, its limited LGBTQ organizations, legal support, tourist infrastructure, and anonymity mean a visibly trans visitor is more conspicuous and has less practical recourse after outing, while hormone therapy is not covered publicly and must be arranged privately. No protective local exception is known to distinguish it from the national picture.

regions.name: Kars
regions.basis: Kars is a socially conservative eastern border province with limited LGBTQ visibility, few support organisations or specialist lawyers, and long distances to major centres where advocacy and consular assistance are concentrated. A trans visitor who is outed there faces the national pattern of police identity checks and General Information Gathering detention, segregated and isolating prison placement, no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection, and official rhetoric framing LGBTQ people as a threat to family and children. Local conservatism and thin recourse increase risks of public harassment, service refusal, and ineffective complaints, while eastern border policing adds scrutiny at checkpoints and crossings.

regions.name: Kastamonu
regions.basis: Kastamonu inherits Turkey's national regime, under which there is no specific border bar for trans visitors but police identity checks, documented street detentions and background recording, segregation and isolation of trans prisoners, and raids and stigmatising official rhetoric create exposure after arrival, with no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection and hormone care available only privately. Locally, Kastamonu is a conservative, inland province centred on a small city with little foreign tourism, no visible trans community or support organisations, and limited legal or medical recourse compared with Istanbul and Ankara. A visitor discovered there would face heightened social hostility and curiosity, fewer witnesses or advocates, and ready police documentation, without any documented local exception to national practice.

regions.name: Kayseri
regions.basis: Kayseri, a socially conservative inland provincial capital in central Anatolia, sits under Turkey's national regime of police identity checks, 'General Information Gathering' documentation, no legal protection on gender identity, and segregation rather than gender-matched placement in detention. Locally, there are few visible trans or LGBTQ venues, limited specialist legal or medical support, and a more conservative host environment than Istanbul, Ankara or Izmir, with public pride events banned under national practice. Foreign tourism is limited mainly to transit and winter-sports visitors, so a traveller discovered as trans would likely face street harassment, police questioning and detention, with little practical recourse locally.

regions.name: Kilis
regions.basis: Kilis inherits Turkey's national regime for a transgender visitor who is outed: no comprehensive protection against gender-identity discrimination, routine identity checks at transit and police stops, documented street detentions and GBT background checks in 2025, prison segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, and official rhetoric and raids framing LGBTQ people as a threat to the family. Kilis adds a small, socially conservative border-province environment on the Syrian frontier, with heavy security presence, frequent checkpoint scrutiny, limited anonymity, and no local LGBTQ support or legal-aid infrastructure comparable to Istanbul, Ankara or Izmir, making discovery more likely to lead to police attention, service refusal and social hostility with recourse distant in Diyarbakir or larger cities.

regions.name: Uşak
regions.basis: Uşak is a province in western Turkey where a transgender visitor, once identified, faces the same national conditions as elsewhere in Turkey: police identity checks and General Information Gathering can lead to detention and documentation, there is no comprehensive ban on discrimination based on gender identity, prison placement follows segregation rather than gender identity, and state rhetoric and raids against LGBTQ organisations have intensified hostility. Hormone therapy is not covered publicly, requiring private arrangements. No region-specific information distinguishes Uşak from the national picture, including any local exemption, protective practice, or documented pattern different from Turkey's overall regime for visitors.

regions.name: Van
regions.basis: Van inherits Turkey's national regime: no entry ban for transgender visitors, but mandatory ID checks at checkpoints, no legal protection based on gender identity, and police use of GBT background checks that have detained trans women in grouped street stops. If detained, trans prisoners face segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, restricted healthcare, arbitrary searches and ineffective complaints. In Van, these national exposures combine with a socially conservative, Kurdish-majority provincial environment, a heavy security and border checkpoint presence, and relatively little visible LGBTQ support, legal aid or advocacy infrastructure compared with Istanbul and Ankara. Tourist activity around Lake Van does not displace those conditions, so discovery is more likely to lead to outing, detention and hostile local treatment with limited practical recourse.

regions.name: Yozgat
regions.basis: Yozgat inherits Turkey's national regime, in which street identity checks and police detention of trans people are documented, a draft package would criminalise advocacy contrary to biological sex, there is no comprehensive gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and prisons segregate trans prisoners with restricted healthcare and ineffective complaints. Locally, Yozgat is a small, socially conservative, largely rural central Anatolian province with little foreign tourism and no documented LGBT venues, support organisations, legal-aid networks or protective local institutions. A trans visitor who is outed therefore faces a highly visible outsider status, conservative social disapproval and likely harassment or service refusal, with police as the practical authority and recourse centred far away in Ankara or Istanbul. No local exception softens the national exposure.

regions.name: Zonguldak
regions.basis: Zonguldak is a small, socially conservative Black Sea city built around coal mining, with coastal tourism but no large metropolitan anonymity or established LGBTQ venues, support organisations or specialist legal clinics comparable to Istanbul or Ankara. A transgender visitor there is under the Turkish national regime: police identity checks and General Information Gathering detentions documented nationally, no comprehensive gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, official rhetoric framing LGBTQ people as a threat to family and children, and prison placement through segregation and isolation rather than gender identity, with documented ineffective complaints. In a smaller community, being outed is more readily visible to officials, employers and neighbours, and access to lawyers and independent oversight is more distant.

regions.name: Çanakkale
regions.basis: Çanakkale inherits Turkey's national regime: no entry ban, but photo ID must be carried at checkpoints in holiday destinations, police can conduct GBT background checks and document visibly trans people, there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection, and trans prisoners are segregated rather than placed according to identity. Locally, the western coastal province is heavily touristed around Gallipoli, Troy and the Dardanelles ferries, is comparatively secular and accustomed to foreign visitors, and has no locally documented pattern of sweeps comparable to Istanbul. That tourist, coastal character may reduce routine street targeting, but ferry and site checkpoints keep document checks frequent, and national detention, healthcare and prison practices apply unchanged if a visitor is outed.

regions.name: Şanlıurfa
regions.basis: Şanlıurfa inherits Turkey's national regime of police identity checks, documented detentions of trans women, segregation in custody, no anti-discrimination protection, and official rhetoric framing LGBTQ people as a threat to family and children. Locally, the province is markedly more socially conservative and religious than Istanbul or western cities, with little visible LGBTQ presence, no Pride events, and fewer legal-aid or support organisations able to intervene after police contact. Tourism centres around Göbeklitepe and Balıklıgöl, but visitors outside those sites have limited anonymity in tight-knit communities, increasing the likelihood that discovery leads to harassment, police referral, or refusal of services, with recourse slower and less effective than in major cities.

regions.name: Şırnak
regions.basis: Şırnak inherits Turkey's national conditions: no entry ban for transgender visitors, but frequent identity checks, documented police detentions of trans women in Istanbul, no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, segregated prison placement with reported abuse, and official rhetoric framing LGBT people as a threat to family and children. Locally, Şırnak is a conservative, predominantly Kurdish, rural border province with a heavy security presence, frequent checkpoints, very limited tourism and almost no visible transgender community or support organisations. Once outed, a visitor would face stronger social hostility, family and community pressure, and less practical access to lawyers, NGOs or medical continuity than in major western cities, with little local recourse if harassed or detained.

regions.name: Funafuti
regions.basis: Funafuti, Tuvalu's capital and main air and sea gateway, concentrates its border control, police, main hospital, government offices and most foreign residents and visitors. A transgender visitor will encounter Tuvalu's unenforced colonial-era felony provisions on male homosexual conduct, with no gender-identity protection and no trans-specific facilities or detention rules documented nationally. Society is predominantly conservative Christian and tightly knit, so discovery is likely to become widely known quickly through gossip and church community, producing curiosity, disapproval and possible service friction, although Tuvalu's traditional pinapinaaine, people assigned male at birth living as women, have a recognised social presence. No local exception to national law applies in Funafuti.

regions.name: Nanumanga
regions.basis: Nanumanga is a small, remote outer atoll in Tuvalu's northwest with a close-knit, predominantly Christian subsistence community, infrequent inter-island transport, and no local legal regime or trans-specific services distinct from the national picture. The inherited national regime retains dormant felony provisions criminalising male same-sex conduct, with no documented prosecutions in the record, and provides no gender-identity protection, while Tuvalu has a longstanding pinapinaaine gender-diverse tradition and recent official recognition of transgender people in health planning. In Nanumanga, discovery would be highly visible in a small community where anonymity is limited and movement off-island is slow, with social and religious disapproval a likely response and formal recourse requiring travel to Funafuti, but no documented local pattern of policing, detention or violence directed at gender-diverse visitors.

regions.name: Nanumea
regions.basis: Nanumea is a small, remote outer atoll in Tuvalu where daily life is organised around kinship, customary chiefs and a strongly Christian community, with very limited anonymity and only a small local clinic before evacuation to Funafuti. Tuvalu's colonial-era Penal Code still criminalises male same-sex intercourse as a felony, though documented enforcement against consenting adults is absent, and no law protects gender identity or expression, regulates facilities by birth sex, or targets gender presentation itself. A visibly transgender visitor would likely be recognised quickly, face intense curiosity, moral disapproval from church and family networks, and possible service friction, with no local advocacy, formal complaint route or protective infrastructure. Police presence is minimal and there is no documented pattern of arrests, custody abuse or violence against transgender people.

regions.name: Niutao
regions.basis: Niutao is a small, remote Tuvaluan atoll with a few hundred residents, a church-centred communal life, limited services and very little tourism, so a visitor cannot expect anonymity. It inherits Tuvalu's national regime: male same-sex conduct remains criminalised under colonial-era penal provisions, though no prosecutions of consenting adults were documented as of 2013, and there is no gender-identity protection, hate-crime law or recorded trans-specific violence data. Outside Funafuti, policing, legal help and medical care are distant and thin. If outed, a trans visitor would likely face intense local scrutiny and social disapproval in a close-knit community with little practical recourse.

regions.name: Nukufetau
regions.basis: Nukufetau is a small, remote Tuvaluan atoll with a close-knit, strongly Christian communal life, where a visibly transgender visitor would be highly conspicuous and have limited anonymity, local services, or recourse, with infrequent transport to Funafuti. Tuvalu's Penal Code sections 153-155 criminalise male homosexual intercourse as felonies carrying up to 14 years, still in force but documented as unenforced with no prosecutions of consenting adults, and a transgender woman read as male by police falls within their terms. No law protects gender identity or expression, and same-sex marriage was constitutionally banned in 2023. A small recognised pinapinaaine presence exists, but traditional customs remain socially conservative and there is no documented trans-specific violence or police targeting.

regions.name: Nukulaelae
regions.basis: Tuvalu criminalises male homosexual intercourse and related acts as felonies, with trans women read as male falling within their scope if outed, although the available record documents no prosecutions of consenting adults and no trans-specific offence, targeting, or detention practice. Workplace law covers sexual orientation but no law covers gender identity or expression, and same-sex relationships have no recognition. Traditional pinapinaaine presence is noted nationally, without documented hate-crime or custody findings. No region-specific information distinguishes Nukulaelae from the national picture, so its conditions are assessed on that inherited regime alone.

regions.name: Vaitupu
regions.basis: Vaitupu is a small, remote outer atoll in Tuvalu, governed by the national law which retains colonial-era felony provisions on male homosexual intercourse, attempts and gross indecency between males, with no documented prosecutions in the available record, and no trans-specific criminal offence, gender-identity protection, or documented police targeting of transgender people. Tuvalu recognises a small traditional pinapinaaine population. Locally, Vaitupu is a tight-knit, church-centred community with very limited anonymity, tourism or medical and legal infrastructure, and distance from Funafuti authorities. A foreign visitor would be highly visible, and discovery would likely bring intense social scrutiny within the community, with limited practical recourse on the atoll, though no local pattern of violence, detention or state enforcement is documented.

regions.name: Iringa
regions.basis: Tanzania criminalises same-sex sexual conduct with penalties up to life imprisonment and gross indecency offences, and law and officials have been used to target LGBTI people through raids, forced anal examinations, deportations and online blocking. A transgender activist was abducted and brutally beaten in 2024, and torture in police custody has been documented. Facilities, documents and custody offer no recognised protection based on gender identity, and medical and public services provide no reliable recourse if a visitor is outed. Iringa, a largely rural southern-highlands centre and gateway to safari areas, has no region-specific information distinguishing it from the national picture; no local exception, protective practice or lighter enforcement is documented.

regions.name: North Pemba
regions.basis: North Pemba, in the Zanzibar archipelago, operates under Zanzibar's separate penal law, which criminalises same-sex conduct and broadly defined gross indecency, with imprisonment penalties, and offers no legal recognition for same-sex partners. The island is predominantly rural and socially conservative, with a close-knit Muslim fishing and farming population, limited large-scale tourism infrastructure outside parts of the south, and less anonymity or specialist legal and medical support than Unguja or the mainland. A transgender visitor who is discovered would face police involvement, detention, extortion or prosecution risks, and strong community hostility with little practical recourse, health care continuity, or privacy in a small-island setting.

regions.name: South Pemba
regions.basis: South Pemba lies in Zanzibar's Pemba island, under Zanzibar's separate penal regime, which criminalises same-sex conduct and broadly defined gross indecency, within a national context of life imprisonment for same-sex acts between men on the mainland, documented police-custody torture and forced examinations, state-led anti-LGBT campaigns, and a severe 2024 attack on a Tanzanian transgender activist. South Pemba is more socially conservative, rural and closely knit than Zanzibar's tourist centre, with little trans-specific protective infrastructure and legal-aid or advocacy support concentrated elsewhere. Discovery would therefore risk arrest, extortion, violence and outing in a small community with limited recourse.

regions.name: Central Region
regions.basis: Central Region includes Kampala, the capital, and surrounding Wakiso and Mukono districts, where state institutions, police headquarters, embassies, hospitals and LGBTQ support networks are concentrated. The national Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 remains in force after constitutional court upholding, including death penalty for aggravated homosexuality and long prison terms for homosexuality, with documented arrests, shelter raids, digital entrapment and invasive examinations, largely reported from Kampala. A transgender woman was mobbed in Kampala in 2024, and a 2021 raid there led to 44 arrests. Urban anonymity, foreigner presence and access to care or consular help may offer limited mitigation, but visibility also brings intensive policing, surveillance and hostile public exposure, while rural parts of the region have little recourse.

regions.name: Cherkasy Oblast
regions.basis: Transgender status is not criminalised in Ukraine, and visitors encounter the same national document, border and mobilisation-check regime as elsewhere, including stops of male-marker holders at crossings and checkpoint scrutiny under martial law. Cherkasy Oblast is largely rural and socially conservative, with a smaller, less visible LGBTQ community and fewer specialist legal-aid and support services than Kyiv or western hubs. Attitudes outside Cherkasy city tend toward greater curiosity and disapproval, police familiarity with gender-identity cases is limited, and there is no separate local protection. Daily life is generally orderly and away from front-line fighting, but being outed is more likely to draw local attention with less institutional support nearby.

regions.name: Chernivtsi Oblast
regions.basis: Chernivtsi Oblast inherits Ukraine's national regime for a transgender visitor: being trans is not criminalised, legal gender recognition does not require surgery, but gender identity is not covered as a hate-crime aggravator in the Criminal Code, workplace and media protections are partial, and family law remains contested. Under martial law, State Border Guard Service checks of male markers at crossings add a specific exposure, and mobilisation exemption remains unresolved. Locally, this southwestern border oblast, with large Romanian and Moldovan minorities and a predominantly Orthodox, socially conservative rural population, has lower LGBTQ visibility and fewer support services than Kyiv or Lviv. Chernivtsi city, a university centre, is comparatively more tolerant, but outside it discovery is more likely to meet disapproval, limited recourse, and intensified scrutiny at frequent Romanian and Moldovan border crossings.

regions.name: Khmelnytskyi Oblast
regions.basis: Ukraine does not criminalise being transgender, and legal gender recognition is available without surgery, though diagnosis remains a reported barrier and gender identity is not covered as a hate-crime ground in criminal law. Under martial law, visitors with male passport markers face border stops and mobilisation-related scrutiny, and family recognition remains contested. Khmelnytskyi Oblast is a non-frontline region in western Ukraine, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture, with no documented local laws, targeted enforcement, or separate protective measures for visitors.

regions.name: Kirovohrad Oblast
regions.basis: Transgender identity is not criminalised in Ukraine, legal gender recognition is available without surgery, and workplace and media discrimination based on gender identity are formally prohibited, while gender identity is not yet a hate-crime aggravating ground in the Criminal Code and protection in practice remains uneven. Under martial law, travellers with male passport markers face border stops and mobilisation-related scrutiny, with no clear trans-specific exemption. Societal attitudes are mixed and police responses to past anti-LGBT violence were often inadequate. No region-specific information distinguishes Kirovohrad Oblast from the national picture in law, enforcement, border practice, facilities, or documented targeting of transgender visitors, and its central, largely non-tourist character provides no documented local exception or additional protective regime.

regions.name: Poltava Oblast
regions.basis: Transgender identity is not criminalised in Ukraine, with legal gender recognition available without surgery, but criminal law does not treat gender identity as a hate-crime aggravating factor, workplace and media protections are partial, and family law remains contested. Under martial law, holders of male markers face document checks and mobilisation-related stops, and official responses to anti-LGBT violence have historically been weak. Poltava Oblast, in central Ukraine away from the capital and western regions, is more rural and socially conservative, with fewer visible support services or LGBTQ venues, so a visitor who is outed is more likely to encounter curiosity, misgendering and service friction, with limited local recourse, while facing no trans-specific imprisonment or execution risk.

regions.name: Rivne Oblast
regions.basis: Rivne Oblast in northwestern Ukraine inherits the national framework, under which being transgender is not criminalised, legal gender recognition is available without surgery, and gender identity is protected in employment and media law, while criminal law does not treat gender identity as a hate-crime aggravating ground and police responses to anti-LGBT violence have historically been weak. Martial-law border controls add document scrutiny for travellers with male markers. Locally, the oblast is predominantly rural and socially conservative, with strong Orthodox influence, a comparatively small urban centre in Rivne, and little visible LGBT community infrastructure or tourism-facing experience outside main cities. A visitor who is recognised as transgender is therefore more likely to encounter curiosity, disapproval and bureaucratic confusion, with fewer affirming services or legal-aid networks nearby than in Kyiv, while facing no local criminal penalty for gender expression.

regions.name: Vinnytsia Oblast
regions.basis: Ukraine does not criminalise being transgender, and legal gender recognition is available without surgery, though diagnosis remains a barrier and transsexuality is still classified as a psychiatric disorder. There is no hate-crime provision covering gender identity, employment discrimination is banned but enforcement and police response to anti-LGBT violence have historically been weak, and family recognition remains contested. Under martial law, holders of male markers face border stops and mobilisation-related scrutiny. Vinnytsia Oblast in central Ukraine has no region-specific information distinguishing it from the national picture: no separate local law, documented local tolerance exception, or harsher local enforcement regime is known, so visitors there encounter the same national conditions as elsewhere.

regions.name: Volyn Oblast
regions.basis: Volyn Oblast operates under Ukraine's national regime: being transgender is not criminalised, documents can be changed without surgery, and workplace and media discrimination based on gender identity are formally prohibited, but gender identity is not a hate-crime aggravating ground in the Criminal Code. Martial-law border checks for holders of male markers, wartime barriers to diagnosis and care, and historically tolerated anti-LGBT violence and police inaction remain relevant exposures if a visitor is outed. Locally, Volyn is a largely rural, religious and socially conservative northwestern border region centred on Lutsk, with less visible LGBT infrastructure and support services than Kyiv or Lviv and greater likelihood of social friction in smaller communities. No separate local law, protective regime, or documented local targeting campaign distinguishes it.

regions.name: Zakarpattia Oblast
regions.basis: Transgender status is not criminalised in Ukraine, and legal gender recognition does not require surgery, but gender identity is not a hate-crime aggravator, police response to anti-LGBT violence has historically been weak, and martial-law border controls stop holders of male markers. Zakarpattia, on the Slovak, Hungarian and Romanian borders, has frequent crossings where those document checks apply. Locally it is more rural and religiously conservative than Kyiv, with strong Greek-Catholic and Orthodox influence, traditional attitudes in many towns and villages, and little LGBTQ support infrastructure outside Uzhhorod. A trans visitor who is outed there is more likely to face staring, refusal or harassment with limited recourse, while imprisonment for being transgender is not the national regime.

regions.name: Zhytomyr Oblast
regions.basis: Zhytomyr Oblast is a largely rural, predominantly Ukrainian-speaking region in northwestern Ukraine, centred on Zhytomyr city with smaller towns and villages where social networks are tight and LGBTQ visibility and support infrastructure are limited compared with Kyiv. Ukrainian national law applies throughout: being trans is not criminalised, legal gender recognition does not require surgery, but gender identity is not a hate-crime aggravator and protections remain partial, with documented police inaction in past attacks. Martial-law checkpoints and border controls, though Zhytomyr is not a frontline oblast, can expose a visitor whose documents and presentation differ, particularly for holders of male markers subject to mobilisation checks. No local punitive statutes, armed-group control, or distinct trans-targeting regime are known, but fewer legal-aid and community resources mean recourse would likely be thinner and more socially exposed than in the capital.

regions.name: Canelones
regions.basis: Canelones is Uruguay's peri-urban department ringing Montevideo, including the Costa de Oro beach towns, La Paz, Las Piedras and other commuter communities closely integrated with the capital, and is governed by the same national framework throughout Uruguay. The 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans People, self-declaration legal gender recognition, hate-crime enhancements and anti-discrimination protections apply without departmental variation, and prison placement, health-care respect and document practices follow national policy. Enforcement and social attitudes are broadly as in Montevideo, with greater tolerance in tourist and metropolitan areas and more uneven service experiences in smaller or rural localities, but no documented local targeting, facility exclusion or separate restrictions distinguish a visitor's experience there from the national picture.

regions.name: Maldonado
regions.basis: Uruguay's national framework applies across Maldonado: self-declared legal gender change without medical requirements, statutory protection in health and public services, hate-crime penalties covering gender identity, legal same-sex relations, and prison placement by the person's choice. Maldonado is dominated socially and economically by Punta del Este and the Atlantic coast, a wealthy, seasonal, international resort area where foreign visitors are routine, nightlife and hospitality workforces are highly cosmopolitan, and events such as Punta Pride are established. That tourist-facing character reduces everyday scrutiny compared with smaller inland towns, which are more socially conservative. Enforcement remains uneven, illustrated by a 2024 discrimination complaint at San Carlos hospital that remained pending, but courts, police and health authorities operate under the national protections.

regions.name: Andijan Region
regions.basis: Andijan inherits Uzbekistan's national regime, under which consensual sexual conduct between men is criminalised and used by police to target gay and bisexual men and trans women through arbitrary detention, prosecution, forced examinations, bribery, blackmail and coercion to inform, with impunity for ill-treatment and no legal protection. LGBTI organisations cannot register and official and societal hostility is documented. In the Fergana Valley, and Andijan in particular, socially conservative, close-knit mahalla communities, strong family and honour norms, limited foreign tourism and support infrastructure, and a heavy security presence mean discovery is more likely to reach police and community actors and less likely to find tolerance, remedy or safe recourse. No local protective exception distinguishes the region.

regions.name: Fergana Region
regions.basis: A transgender visitor discovered in Fergana Region faces the same national criminal framework as elsewhere in Uzbekistan, where consensual male same-sex conduct carries imprisonment and police have targeted trans women with detention, prosecution, forced examinations described as torture, extortion and impunity. Conditions in the densely populated Fergana Valley add local pressure: the region is socially and religiously conservative, community and neighbourhood oversight is strong, and visible gender diversity has little public acceptance or protective infrastructure compared with the capital. There is no local exception to national enforcement, no effective legal recourse, and official hostility remains nationwide.

regions.name: Namangan Region
regions.basis: Uzbekistan criminalises consensual sex between men under Article 120, with documented prosecutions, and police are reported to target trans women with arbitrary detention, extortion and forced examinations amounting to torture, with impunity for ill-treatment and no legal protection. Namangan lies in the Fergana Valley, a more socially conservative and religious, largely rural region with little international tourism infrastructure or visible trans community compared with Tashkent. A foreign visitor who is outed there would therefore be conspicuous, face strong community and family-related hostility, and have little practical recourse to police, courts or registered support organisations. No local protective exception to the national regime is known.

regions.name: Charlotte
regions.basis: Charlotte is a parish on the windward coast of Saint Vincent, centred on Georgetown, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture. The inherited regime criminalises consensual sex between men under sections 146 and 148, with penalties up to ten and five years, upheld by the High Court in February 2024. There is no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, no dedicated LGBT organisation or helpline, and documented bias-motivated violence and stigma, including attacks on cross-dressing people and a 2019 fraud charge after a transphobic assault. No special entry rule for LGBT travellers is documented.

regions.name: Grenadines
regions.basis: The Grenadines are a chain of small, tourism- and yachting-oriented islands within Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, whose criminal code criminalises consensual sex between men under sections 146 and 148, with penalties up to ten and five years, upheld by the High Court in February 2024. No law protects against discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no local LGBT support organisation or helpline is documented. Social life is small and close-knit, churches are conservative, and trans people face stigma and possible harassment, although resort and expatriate enclaves encounter more foreign visitors. Enforcement against visitors is not documented, but the same statutes, absence of recourse, and limited local services apply throughout the islands.

regions.name: Saint Andrew
regions.basis: Saint Andrew is a rural west-coast parish centred on villages such as Barrouallie and Layou, with fishing, farming and hiking tourism rather than the anonymity of Kingstown. A transgender visitor outed here faces the national regime: consensual male same-sex conduct remains criminalised under sections 146 and 148, upheld by the High Court in 2024, with no sexual-orientation or gender-identity anti-discrimination protection and no recognised same-sex union. National reporting documents bias-motivated harassment and a 2019 cross-dressing teenager assaulted then charged with fraud for presenting as a woman, the charge later withdrawn. Locally, close-knit, church-influenced communities offer less privacy and fewer support services, and there is no documented local tolerance or protective exceptions distinguishing the parish.

regions.name: Saint David
regions.basis: Transgender visitors in Saint David fall under the same national regime as the rest of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, with no region-specific information distinguishing the parish from the national picture. Consensual sex between men remains criminalised under sections 146 and 148, upheld by the High Court in February 2024, and no law prohibits discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Documented bias-motivated violence and discrimination, attacks on cross-dressing young men in 2018, and a 2019 case in which a cross-dressing teenager was assaulted then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman illustrate exposure if outed. There is no LGBT organisation, helpline or dedicated support service, and LGBT life remains stigmatised and largely invisible.

regions.name: Saint George
regions.basis: Saint George is the capital of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and no region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture. The inherited regime criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under sections 146 and 148, with penalties of up to ten and five years respectively, upheld by the High Court in February 2024. There is no law prohibiting discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no organisation dedicated to LGBT people operates in the country. Documented bias-motivated violence includes attacks on cross-dressing young men and a teenager who was assaulted and then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman, a charge later withdrawn. A trans visitor discovered in Saint George therefore faces stigma, possible arrest and prosecution, and little recourse.

regions.name: Saint Patrick
regions.basis: Saint Patrick in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines operates under the national legal regime applying across the country, and no region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture. Consensual same-sex conduct between men remains criminalised under sections 146 and 148 of the criminal code, upheld by the High Court in February 2024, with no law protecting against discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Documented cases show cross-dressing people facing physical attacks and, in 2019, a cross-dressing teenager assaulted and then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman before the charge was withdrawn. Social infrastructure for LGBT people is thin and visibility low, leaving a visitor who is discovered without dedicated support or legal recourse.

regions.name: Anzoátegui
regions.basis: Anzoátegui, on Venezuela's eastern Caribbean coast, is subject to the same national regime as the rest of the country. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, but there is no hate-crime statute or anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no working route to documents matching gender identity. Police action has nevertheless included raids on LGBTQ venues, extortion and baseless accusations related to homosexuality, with little effective recourse for victims. No region-specific information distinguishes Anzoátegui from the national picture in relation to border or document treatment, public facilities, police conduct, violence, or healthcare access for a transgender visitor who is discovered.

regions.name: Barinas
regions.basis: Barinas is a largely rural state in western Venezuela with limited tourist infrastructure and few large urban centres, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture. Across Venezuela consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, but there is no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination law, no working route to obtain local identity documents matching gender identity, and documented police raids on LGBTQ venues involving warrantless entry and extortion have occurred nationally. A visitor discovered as transgender would rely on foreign documents, face possible invasive questioning or harassment without dedicated legal recourse, and have limited local support organisations or protective institutions in this less urbanised state.

regions.name: Bolívar
regions.basis: A transgender visitor in Bolívar is governed by the Venezuelan national regime, with no region-specific information distinguishing the state from the national picture. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised and the age of consent is 16, but there is no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination law, and no working legal gender recognition route, so foreign documents cannot be replaced locally. Police action has included a 2026 raid in Barquisimeto in which about 30 people were detained, allegedly extorted and accused of 'homosexuality' despite no such crime. Institutional protections remain limited despite symbolic anti-homophobia measures and early LGBT parliamentary representation, leaving recourse for violence, discrimination or police abuse weak.

regions.name: Carabobo
regions.basis: Carabobo, centered on Valencia and including the port of Puerto Cabello, operates under Venezuela's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalized, but there is no hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and no functioning route for documents matching gender identity. National reporting includes a 2026 raid in neighboring Lara in which about 30 people were detained at an LGBTQ+ venue, allegedly without proper warrants, with extortion and unfounded accusations of homosexuality. No region-specific information distinguishes Carabobo's treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture, and no local protective or harsher enforcement regime is known.

regions.name: Cojedes
regions.basis: Cojedes is a small, largely rural inland state in Venezuela's central plains, centred on San Carlos, with no region-specific information distinguishing it from the national picture for a transgender visitor. The inherited national regime applies: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, but there is no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination law, no working legal gender recognition route, and no Venezuelan documents matching gender identity are available to a visitor. Police raids and extortion at LGBTQ venues have been documented elsewhere in Venezuela, with no dedicated penalty for anti-trans violence or discrimination. No local protective institutions, facility rules, or documented tolerance specific to Cojedes are known.

regions.name: Delta Amacuro
regions.basis: Venezuela does not criminalise same-sex conduct, but provides no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, no functioning route for documents matching gender identity, and police elsewhere have raided an LGBTQ+ venue, detained about 30 people, and extorted them under a baseless charge. Delta Amacuro adds remoteness rather than protection: a small, sparsely populated Orinoco Delta state centred on Tucupita, with riverine Warao and rural Creole communities, limited tourism and transport, thin police and judicial presence, and scarce hospital and pharmacy services. A visitor who is outed would face the same document and recourse gaps nationally, with longer distances to legal help, consular support and hormone continuity, and fewer local organisations or protective services to intervene.

regions.name: Dependencias Federales
regions.basis: Dependencias Federales comprises small, sparsely populated offshore islands administered under Venezuelan national law, with no separate legal regime for transgender visitors. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, but there is no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination statute, no working route to legal gender recognition or matching national documents, and limited institutional protection. National reporting documents police raids on LGBTQ venues, warrantless entry, extortion and baseless accusations, with weak accountability. No region-specific information distinguishes the treatment of a transgender visitor who is outed there from the national picture; no distinct local protections or additional trans-specific enforcement are known.

regions.name: Distrito Capital
regions.basis: Caracas, in Distrito Capital, is Venezuela's most urban and internationally connected centre, with the country's largest visible transgender community, LGBTQ venues neighborhood life, Pride events and national advocacy organisations concentrated there, alongside embassies and media that can publicise abuse. It inherits the national position of no criminalisation of same-sex conduct but no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination protection and no working route to matching local documents. Police harassment and extortion under unfounded morality allegations, documented elsewhere in Venezuela, remain a risk in a capital with dense security checkpoints and political policing, and victims have little effective legal recourse if outed.

regions.name: Guárico
regions.basis: Venezuela does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct, but it has no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination law, and police have raided an LGBTQ venue, detained about 30 people, and allegedly extorted them under a non-existent homosexuality charge, showing law on the books does not reliably protect visibly gender-nonconforming visitors. Guárico, in the central llanos, operates under the same national authorities, courts, and police structures, with no separate entry, document, or facility regime. No region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture, and no local protective machinery or documented targeting pattern is known to alter the inherited exposure.

regions.name: La Guaira
regions.basis: La Guaira shares Venezuela's national legal and institutional regime, and no region-specific information distinguishes its treatment of transgender people from the national picture. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, but there is no hate-crime statute or anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and nationally police have raided LGBTQ venues, extorted and detained people under unfounded accusations. Legal gender recognition is effectively unavailable, official protection is limited and suspended where proclaimed, and weak rule of law means complaints and remedies are unreliable. An outed visitor therefore faces harassment, arbitrary police action and service discrimination with little effective recourse.

regions.name: Lara
regions.basis: Venezuela does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and has no statute criminalising gender expression, but it provides no hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection for gender identity and no working route for documents matching gender identity, leaving a trans visitor to rely on home documents. In Lara, documented local enforcement is the key exposure: in May 2026 police raided an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto without proper warrants, detained about thirty people, extorted them and accused them of 'homosexuality', a non-existent offence. Barquisimeto is a more socially conservative provincial capital than Caracas, with thinner legal-aid and advocacy recourse. No local protective regime, facility, custody or care protection is documented; police are documented perpetrators rather than protectors.

regions.name: Monagas
regions.basis: Monagas, in eastern Venezuela, shares the national legal position: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, but there is no hate-crime or gender-identity anti-discrimination law, no functioning legal gender recognition, and a visitor's foreign documents would not be matched by Venezuelan records. Police abuse against LGBTQ+ venues, including a 2026 raid in Lara involving warrantless entry, extortion and unfounded accusations, illustrates a national pattern of discretionary detention without a legal basis.
